Safe and ethical use is promoted through content filtering， monitoring student interactions and teaching responsible use， academic integrity， and the risks of misuse， such as plagiarism. Student well-being is supported by preventing over-reliance on AI， addressing misinformation， managing screen time and considering social and emotional impacts. Implementation is handled thoughtfully with thorough training for teachers， clear policies， regular evaluation and adaptation of safety practices， and active involvement from all stakeholders. Learn About AI Together: Take some time to explore what AI is and how it’s being used in education. Understanding its benefits and challenges will help you guide your child. Have Open Conversations: Discuss with your child how to use AI responsibly and ethically. Help them understand the importance of critical thinking and creativity while using AI tools. Stay Connected with Teachers: Talk to your child’s teachers about how AI is being used in the classroom. This ensures you're both on the same page and can reinforce healthy AI habits at home. title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidance (Cherry Creek School District)
full_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidance Cherry Creek Schools believes in empowering students， staff， and the community to engage with artificial intelligence in safe， smart， and social ways that support our core values. Continuous learning and adaptation keep students and staff future-ready. As AI evolves， we refine our practices and grow our understanding to meet what comes next. Every learner deserves fair access to tools that support success. AI should reduce barriers， not reinforce them， so all students and staff can achieve their full potential. Keeping student and staff information safe builds trust and creates a secure environment where learning can thrive. When people feel protected， they are more willing to explore， think， and grow. Students and staff grow when they think deeply， make decisions， and create original work. AI should enhance curiosity and learning while reinforcing a growth mindset. The Delaware Council on Educational Technology presents this guidance to support educators and education leaders in the appropriate， equitable， and inclusive use of AI in classrooms across the State of Delaware. Included in this Guidance Document Understanding AI Delve into artificial intelligence， clarify its definition， weigh the advantages and disadvantages of its use in education， and dispel common myths surrounding its capabilities and limitations. Implementing Generative AI in Delaware Districts and Charters The comprehensive recommendations address crucial policy areas such as protecting student data， ensuring ethical， equitable， and effective Generative AI use， promoting equity， and enhancing learning through content and curricula that leverage Generative AI technologies. Best practices are provided with implementation strategies， suggestions for managing platforms， and tools for evaluating Generative AI products. Integrating Generative AI into the Classroom This section provides optimal practices for integrating Generative AI within the classroom. It emphasizes applications and strategies to enhance educational experiences， demonstrating how tools and applications support teaching and learning processes. The SAMR model includes illustrations to show how applications may align to each level. Also included are strategies for addressing academic dishonesty and ensuring that Generative AI tools are used responsibly in educational settings. Professional Learning The final section suggests a framework for professional learning， listing essential topics and subject areas on which school districts and charter schools may choose to focus. Scalable training and delivery methods are recommended to guarantee that all educators and students across Delaware have equal opportunities to benefit from Generative AI technologies. This approach aims to equip teachers with the knowledge and skills necessary to integrate Generative AI into their teaching practices effectively， thereby enhancing the educational experience for students. 5 How to Use This Guidance Document The guidance issued by the Delaware Council on Educational Technology on the adoption of Generative AI in educational settings serves as a comprehensive resource for educators and leaders across the state: School District and Charter School leaders may use this guidance to support incorporating AI into their local policies (e.g.， responsible use， academic integrity， etc.). School District and Charter School leaders and classroom educators are provided with this guidance as a source of support， resources， and established best practices for integrating AI technologies within their instructional environments. 6 Understanding Artificial Intelligence The advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within the educational sphere marks a pivotal shift towards integrating technology that complements human intelligence and enriches the humanitarian essence of learning. The burgeoning influence demands a discerning approach to adopting and implementing technological solutions. The educational community must engage in an informed evaluation of AI- driven products， focusing on the mechanics of their operation， the nature of data collection， and the origins of their informational content. This strategy ensures the alignment of technological adoption with core educational values of integrity， safety， and instructional efficacy. One helpful glossary on AI for education is the CIRCLS Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Defining AI AI is not a singular technology but rather a collection of technologies and methodologies to simulate human cognitive processes. These include machine learning， natural language processing (NLP)， robotics， and computer vision. AI systems can analyze large volumes of data， learn from experiences， and perform tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. We have provided the following graphic to provide a common language of terms and themes of AI in the K-12 classroom (Regona et al.， 2022). 7 What is Artificial Intelligence? What is it Not? Artificial Intelligence encompasses a broad range of computer science disciplines aimed at creating machines capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence. These tasks include learning， problem-solving， pattern recognition， and language understanding. While AI augments human capabilities， it does not replicate empathy， creativity， or ethical judgment. Its learning is limited by the data it's trained on， emphasizing the need for critical thinking about its use and limitations. What is AI and What is it Not?? These tasks include learning， problem-solving， pattern recognition， and language understanding. Natural Language Processing (NLP): Not Consciousness: AI understanding and interpreting AI lacks consciousness， emotions， and human language. self-awareness. Adaptive: Not Without Limitations: AI improves its performance based on AI's understanding and operation are experience. confined to its programming. Analytical: Not Infallible: AI extracts insights from large datasets. AI can err， especially with unfamiliar data or scenarios. References: Department of Education Office of Educational Technology. (n.d.). Artificial Intelligence and the future of teaching and learning. Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning. https://tech.ed.gov/files/2023/05/ai-future-of-teaching-and-learning-report.pdf National Institute of Standards and Technology. (2023). Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0). U.S. Department of Commerce. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf 8 Predictive AI Predictive AI uses data about past behaviors to identify patterns and forecast things we might want or do in the future. For example， recommending products people may be interested in purchasing or movies they may be interested in viewing. In education， predictive AI tools may analyze patterns in student data to predict outcomes， but it is important to note that these outputs represent informed guesses， not certainty about the future. Educators must use their human discretion to evaluate potential bias or misconceptions regarding student outcomes. Other uses of predictive AI tools that may already be included are tutors that provide personalized teaching and assistance with administrative tasks such as scheduling (OpenAI， 2023). Defining Generative AI This guidance document focuses on Generative AI in K-12 educational settings. Generative AI refers to tools that produce new content， such as text， images， videos， or music based on patterns they've learned from their training data (OpenAI， 2023). Imagine having a digital assistant who not only helps with grading papers but can also draft creative lesson plans， generate engaging educational content， and even offer personalized learning experiences for each student. Generative AI is like a highly skilled artist that can produce an array of original creations—from paintings to poems to scientific reports—based on its extensive learning from existing works. At its core， Generative AI learns from a vast collection of data. For teachers， this could mean everything from textbooks and scientific journals to novels and historical documents. By analyzing this data， the AI learns patterns， structures， and the essence of the content， enabling it to generate new， original material that aligns with the learned patterns. 9 Generative AI presents a transformative opportunity for educational settings， fostering creativity， critical thinking， and engagement among students through activities such as generating creative writing prompts， solving mathematical problems， or illustrating complex scientific concepts. While these technologies offer exciting possibilities for enhancing K-12 education by serving as powerful tools for learning and creativity， they also pose challenges that require careful navigation. Educators can integrate these technologies more effectively into their classrooms by developing a greater understanding of generative AI's capabilities and limitations. Moreover， fostering a culture of critical thinking and continuous learning among students is crucial for them to adeptly navigate the complexities of AI， preparing them for a future where such technologies play an increasingly significant role (Gianinni， 2023). Generative AI Advantages and Cautions The infographic below highlights some of the advantages and disadvantages of AI in K-12 education. The May 2023 article from the Berkman Klein Center explores the impact of Generative AI in K-12 education， highlighting both advantages and cautions. Advantages include enhancing personalized learning， fostering creativity， and equalizing educational opportunities. Cautions involve exacerbating socioeconomic disparities， challenges in academic integrity， privacy concerns， and the need for critical engagement with AI tools to prevent dependency， among others. It underscores the importance of balancing technological integration with safeguarding educational integrity and equity. 10 AI in K-12 Education Advantages and Cautions What are the advantages? What are the cautions? Efficiency and Speed Privacy Concerns AI can process and analyze data far The use of AI in education involves more quickly than humans， leading to collecting and analyzing vast faster decision-making. amounts of personal data from students， raising significant privacy 24/7 Operation concerns. AI systems can work continuously without breaks or fatigue， unlike Lack of Creativity humans. AI lacks the human capacity for creativity and can only generate Error Reduction output based on its programming AI can significantly reduce errors and and training. increase accuracy in data-driven industries. Ethical Concerns AI can perpetuate social biases in training data， leading to unfair or unethical outcomes. 11 Implementing Generative AI for Districts and Charter Schools School districts and charter schools are positioned to leverage Generative AI as a transformative tool within an established framework that prioritizes student safety， educational integrity， and evidence-based instructional methodologies. The integration of Generative AI may not necessitate the creation of new policies but rather the extension of existing policies to address emerging concerns. The journey towards effective Generative AI integration in education begins with a comprehensive understanding of its potential to revolutionize access and utilization of information and enhance learning and work environments. Policies， systems， and instructional practices must be anchored in safety， ethics， equity， and educational standards， ensuring that applications benefit all learners within our communities. Key Policy Areas for Implementation of Generative AI The key policy areas provide a framework for integrating Generative AI technologies within academic settings， ensuring privacy protection， ethical use， and equity to enhance learning. 12 Best Practices for Implementation Strategies Districts and charter schools may develop a multidisciplinary task force to oversee AI integration during implementation planning. This team should be tasked with continuously monitoring AI systems to ensure they operate as intended and update them to reflect new data and ethical standards. Diverse stakeholders should be represented on the task force and engaged in implementing Generative AI to ensure broad perspectives and needs are considered. A clear strategy for ongoing task force communication should be developed. Decisions should be widely distributed to ensure transparency for all stakeholders. District and Charter Schools should consider the following best practices when integrating Generative AI into instruction: Protecting Student Data Establish strict data privacy and security measures to protect PII， especially student information Personally Identifiable Information (PII) should not be manually entered into Generative AI systems Adhere to federal and state laws Ensure the Generative AI vendor complies with signing Delaware Department of Technology & Information (DTI) Terms and Conditions Governing Cloud Services and Data Usage Ensure AI systems are safe， minimizing risks to humans Ensuring Ethical AI Use Accountability for the use of AI systems deployed Evaluate information generated by AI for social bias Promoting Equity Review and revise existing policies to ensure all students have access to AI for enhanced learning opportunities when applicable and appropriate Create equitable outcomes for all users Promote inclusivity Enhancing Learning Select content and resources that integrate pedagogically sound AI and align with educational standards Align educational resources addressing digital citizenship and media literacy， including information on how Generative AI may be used for cyberbullying Stay informed and updated with state terms and conditions for data use， privacy， policies， and legislation. 13 Managing Generative AI Platforms New platforms are launching daily. It is important to note that many of these platforms are interfaces between the user and another Generative AI system， such as OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's Gemini. Districts and charter schools should review each system's terms and conditions and integrations with additional systems before utilizing or adopting them. Steps should be taken to review specific age restrictions， privacy， and student data collection practices within all third-party vendors. As the landscape of education evolves with the integration of Generative AI， it is essential to recognize that educational platforms and tools will undergo rapid changes. Educators， students， and parents are encouraged to stay informed about their rights， responsibilities， and privacy implications of these technologies. Evaluation of AI Platforms & AI Within Existing Platforms Evaluating AI platforms and their integration into existing systems is crucial. It aligns AI deployment with educational goals to improve learning outcomes and ensure equitable access. The Emerging Technology Adoption Framework promotes transparency and accountability. This approach mitigates risks like data privacy and biases and fosters Generative AI’s responsible and ethical use in educational environments. The Emerging Technology Adoption Framework was developed with education community members to ensure educational leaders， tech experts， teachers， students， and their families actively evaluate and adopt new technologies in PK-12 education settings. This initiative was spearheaded by engaging an Emerging Technology Advisory Board via Educator CIRCLS， an entity under The Center for Integrative Research in Computing and Learning Sciences (CIRCLS) (Ruiz and Fusco， 2024). 14 Integration of AI into the Classroom To fully realize Generative AI's potential in education， school districts and charter schools must ensure that educational and technological standards are met， thereby facilitating the use of Generative AI tools to augment educational experiences. State and local policymakers and academic leaders should establish an equitable framework supporting comprehensive policies catering to all students' diverse needs and capabilities. This approach will enable the safe and effective use of tools in learning environments， preparing students for the challenges and opportunities of the future. Protecting Student Data with Generative AI Classroom Integration Integrating Generative AI into K-12 education presents a transformative opportunity to enhance learning experiences and outcomes. However， it necessitates a meticulous approach to protecting student data， ensuring privacy， and maintaining compliance with legal frameworks such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA). School Districts and Charter Schools must prioritize establishing robust data governance policies with precise data collection， storage， access， and sharing protocols. Implementing these tools should be accompanied by rigorous security measures， including encryption and secure authentication， to safeguard against unauthorized access to sensitive information. Furthermore， transparency with students and parents about using Generative AI and the data it generates is crucial. This involves providing accessible information on how data is used to support educational goals and how privacy is protected. By thoughtfully integrating technologies within a framework of strong data protection practices， academic institutions can unlock the potential of Generative AI to personalize learning while simultaneously upholding the trust and confidence of the educational community in the digital age. The Delaware Department of Technology and Information provides terms and conditions for cloud services and student data usage. This documentation needs to be recorded and signed when contracting with vendors. Ensuring Ethical AI Use with AI Classroom Integration Educators must prioritize digital citizenship and media literacy when integrating Generative AI into the classroom to empower students with essential skills for navigating the digital world. Digital Citizenship encompasses diverse skills， fostering an understanding of appropriate， responsible， ethical， and healthy behavior. Media literacy involves accessing， analyzing， evaluating， creating， and taking action with various forms of communication， including AI-generated responses (AIFWD， 2023). 15 Promoting Equity with Generative AI Classroom Integration Adopting Generative AI in education necessitates focusing on ethics， equity， and digital literacy. This involves addressing potential biases in these systems， ensuring data privacy， and promoting an inclusive learning environment that benefits all students. Educational leaders must establish policies and practices reflecting these values， ensuring AI tools are used ethically， equitably， and effectively. Enhancing Learning with Generative AI Classroom Integration Generative AI has the potential to revolutionize learning by providing access to personalized and immersive educational experiences. Examples include using augmented reality (AR) for interactive learning sessions and employing chatbots for tutoring and support. These applications engage students in novel ways and support diverse learning styles and needs， making education more accessible and practical. Integrating Generative AI allows educators to engage students in deep and meaningful learning， promoting high levels of creativity and critical thinking skills. Our role as educators is to educate our students， teaching them how to use Generative AI appropriately to enhance their learning， creativity， and demonstration of standard mastery. 16 Below are some best practices from AIFWD for integrating Generative AI in the classroom. When selecting a Generative AI tool， carefully review the age restrictions， privacy， and data collection policies before implementing them in the classroom. Participate in a classroom discussion on plagiarism and establish guidelines for Generative AI citations. (Citation resources: MLA Style - Generative AI ， APA Style - ChatGPT， and Chicago Style - Generative AI ; OpenAI has a “Get Citation” feature that creates a current citation) Be clear about how and when students are expected to use or not use AI. Permissive: Students freely utilize AI tools to assist in assignments， such as generating ideas， proofreading， or organizing content. Moderate: Students may use AI tools for specific parts of the assignment， such as brainstorming or initial research， but core content and conclusions are original. Restrictive: AI tools are prohibited for the assignment， and all work must be author’s original creation (OpenAI， 2023). Avoid using AI detection tools as they are proven unreliable， often resulting in false positives (e.g.， Checking the Google version history of the document to see if paragraphs have been added in one keystroke). Provide instruction on how students can be critical consumers of Generative AI， evaluating responses to see if they meet their needs and verifying facts， figures， quotes， and data using reliable sources. Consider how Generative AI may be used as a thought partner for students as a brainstorming tool or to provide feedback. Ensure equity by making Generative AI tools available to all students， considering that some may and some may not have access outside of school if an assignment permits use. Provide a blended learning experience integrating technology with discussions， hands-on learning， and project-based assignments and assessments. 17 AI and the SAMR Model The SAMR model， developed by Dr. Ruben Puentedura， provides a framework for incorporating technology into education and categorizes technology integration into four levels: Substitution， Augmentation， Modification， and Redefinition. AI and the SAMR Model The table below illustrates how generative AI applications in the classroom can fit into each level of the SAMR model， as described with examples that may be suited for secondary classrooms. Generative AI and Student Learning As K-12 education systems increasingly integrate Generative AI into the learning environment， it is imperative to harness its transformative potential responsibly and effectively. This guidance document aims to illuminate Generative AI's benefits in enhancing student well-being and improving learning outcomes， as well as the associated risks and strategies for their mitigation. The graphic below outlines AI's potential advantages， related risks， and strategies for mitigating these risks in student learning. 18 Benefits Personalized Content and Review: AI can help generate personalized study materials， summaries， quizzes， and visual aids， help students (including those with disabilities) access and develop tailored resources to meet their specific needs， and help students organize thoughts and review content. Aiding Creativity: Students can harness generative AI as a tool to spark creativity across diverse subjects， including writing， visual arts， and music composition. AI can suggest novel concepts or generate artwork or musical sequences to build upon. Tutoring: AI technologies have the potential to democratize one-to-one tutoring and support， especially for students with financial or geographic constraints. Virtual teaching assistants powered by AI can provide round-the-clock support， help with homework， and supplement classroom instruction. Critical Thinking and Future Skills: Students who learn about how AI works are better prepared for future careers in a wide range of industries. They can develop computational thinking skills to break down complex problems， analyze data critically， and evaluate the effectiveness of solutions. Risks Plagiarism and cheating can occur when students copy from generative AI tools without approval or adequate documentation and submit AI-Generated work as their original work. Misinformation can be produced by Generative AI tools， leading to widespread misconceptions. Bullying and harassment by using AI tools to manipulate media in order to impersonate others can have severe consequences for students' well-being. Overreliance on AI models can lead to undercutting the learning process and abandoning human discretion and oversight. Important nuances and context can be overlooked and accepted. People may overly trust AI outputs， especially when AI is seen as having human-like characteristics. Unequal access to AI tools worsens the digital divide between students with independent and readily available access at home or on personal devices and students dependent on school or community resources. 19 Risk Mitigation In addition to being clear about when and how AI tools may be used to complete assignments， teachers can restructure assignments to reduce opportunities for plagiarism and decrease the benefit of AI tools. This may include evaluating the artifact development process rather than just the final artifact and requiring personal context， original arguments， or original data collection. Students should learn how to critically evaluate all AI-generated content for misinformation or manipulation and be taught about responsible development and sharing of content. Staff and students should be taught how to properly cite and acknowledge the use of AI where applicable. If an assignment permits the use of AI tools， the tools must be made available to all students， considering that some may already have access to such resources outside of school. 20 Professional Learning Opportunities Educators must have the knowledge and skills to effectively integrate Generative AI into teaching and learning processes. These examples of professional learning will equip educators with tools and foundational knowledge to support their classrooms on their journey. Professional Learning Programs These offerings below highlight examples for consideration when implementing your school district or charter school’s professional learning for educators on Generative AI in the K-12 classroom: Generative AI for Teacher and Staff Productivity Training on using AI tools to streamline administrative tasks， improve classroom management， and enhance communication between teachers， staff， and students. This includes automating routine processes， providing insights into student performance， and facilitating resource management. Generative AI for Creatives Explore tools that enhance creative processes in education， focusing on integrating Generative AI tools to support artistic and innovative activities， such as digital art， music composition， and creative writing， helping educators foster creativity in students using cutting-edge technology. Protecting Student Data Prompt Engineering for Educators: Best practices for designing prompts that maximize teacher capacity while protecting student data and PII. Generative AI to Support Pedagogy: Leverage tools for personalized learning， student engagement， and formative assessment to enhance classroom pedagogy and support individual student needs while maintaining student data privacy. Ensuring Ethical Generative AI Use Curriculum Integration: Training on integrating Generative AI tools and resources into the curriculum， including lesson planning and assessment strategies. 21 Connections to Generative AI and Special Education: Training on Generative AI and creating support for exceptional education learners. Discuss goals， protecting student data， privacy dos and don’ts when prompting， and best practices for personalized learning. Promoting Equity Introduction to Bias in Generative AI: Explore Generative AI in K-12 education， focusing on understanding and identifying bias within artificial intelligence systems and a foundational perspective on the impact of social bias on educational content and student interactions. Equitable Access: Providing access to Generative AI tools and making them available for all learners. Enhancing Learning Preparing Students for an AI-Infused Future: The future is now! How can students leverage AI technology to prepare them for their desired futures? Delivery Methods Online courses and webinars for flexible learning. Hands-on workshops and seminars for practical experience. Peer learning groups are used to share experiences and strategies. Content Delivery Resource Examples TeachAI - AI in Education Presentation Slidedeck AI for Education - Downloadable Resources AI for Education - Webinar Series 22 Next Steps in the Process Outline a roadmap for integrating Generative AI into educational systems， emphasizing ongoing evaluation， stakeholder engagement， and adaptive strategies. Short-Term Actions Policy Review and Development: School districts and charter schools can assess current technology policies and develop new guidelines to accommodate Generative AI integration. Pilot Programs: School districts and charter schools can initiate small-scale Generative AI pilot programs to explore potential uses and identify challenges within specific educational contexts. Medium-Term Actions Professional Learning Rollout: School districts and charter schools can expand professional learning programs based on initial feedback and identified needs. Examples include: Generative AI and Connections to The Delaware Digital Citizenship Act and Media Literacy Standards This professional learning centers around Delaware’s Digital Citizenship Act and Media Literacy Standards and how Generative AI can support educators in meeting the needs of all learners throughout K-12. Generative AI Literacy for Educators Courses and/or workshops designed to enhance understanding of Generative AI technologies， their applications in education， and their ethical implications. Long-Term Actions Generative AI Integration: Based on pilot program outcomes and ongoing feedback， school districts and charters roll out integration across more significant segments of the educational system. Continuous Review and Adaptation: school districts and charter schools can establish mechanisms for continuously evaluating Generative AI use in education， ensuring practices remain ethical， equitable， and effective. 23 Conclusion As we conclude our guidance document， the Delaware educational community embarks on a journey toward integrating Generative AI into our educational fabric. This endeavor is not just about keeping pace with technological advancements; it is about redefining the academic landscape to make it more inclusive， innovative， and insightful. With the steadfast support of educators， administrators， and the wider community， we stand at the cusp of a transformative era. Delaware educators' commitment has laid a solid foundation for this next step. Creating a robust tech infrastructure has facilitated a seamless transition to digital learning and primed our schools to integrate technologies. As we move forward， we must approach AI enthusiastically and cautiously， ensuring its incorporation into teaching， learning， and administrative operations enriches the educational experience without overshadowing the human elements essential to learning. Our vision extends beyond the mere use of Generative AI in classrooms. We aim to cultivate an environment where technology enhances communication， collaboration， critical thinking， creativity， engagement， and ethical understanding. By equipping our educators and students with the knowledge and resources to use Generative AI judiciously， we prepare them for future jobs and foster a culture of lifelong learning and curiosity. The journey ahead is not without its challenges. The rapid evolution of this technology demands continuous learning and adaptation. However， by prioritizing professional learning and support for our educators， we can ensure they are well- prepared to guide our students in navigating the complexities of a technology- driven world. 24 References AIFWD. title: Florida K-12 AI Education Task Force - Introduction (CS Everyone Center， University of Florida)
full_text: Introduction Mission Alignment and the Future of Florida Education “The mission of Florida’s Early Learning-20 education system shall be to increase the proficiency of all students within one seamless， efficient system， by allowing them the opportunity to expand their knowledge and skills through learning opportunities and research valued by students， parents， and communities.” This fundamental commitment from the Florida Department of Education anchors the broader vision shared by Florida’s school districts， universities， industry， and stakeholders: to foster a robust， and future-ready society that responsibly embraces emerging technologies and leads in global competitiveness. As Artificial Intelligence (AI) continues its rapid transformation of the way we live and work the Task Force prioritizes the safety in K-12 education as essential to advancing this mission to equip all students with the skills they need to succeed. The integration of AI into Florida’s State Academic Standards for Computer Science ， effective July 2024， represents a significant and foundational step in preparing Florida’s students for an increasingly digital world. Teaching and learning AI is critical not only for student success but also for empowering the entire educational community. The Florida K-12 AI Task Force is committed to harnessing the transformative potential of AI to ensure a safe， responsible， developmentally appropriate， and effective educational environment， grounded in the state’s vision to cultivate informed and responsible digital citizens. Florida Department of Education Computer Science Standards Progression The Florida K-12 standards emphasize skills in the following areas: Computation thinking and reasoning Programming and software engineering Emerging technologies Technological impact Cybersecurity Personal health and safety Communication and collaboration Digital currencies and financial management The FL K-12 AI Task Force leverages Florida’s State Academic Standards for Computer Science when guiding recommendations on effective integration on AI literacy， safety， and ethical use in classrooms. Purpose This guidance document provides a flexible， comprehensive framework for the responsible and effective integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) education across all Florida K-12 settings. Its purpose is to equip all leaders from state level to the community level with the necessary vision， resources， and policy recommendations to ensure that every student is prepared to navigate and shape a world increasingly driven by AI. Navigation and Contributing to the Guidance Our Task Force aims to unify stakeholder efforts and guide Florida’s K–12 AI initiatives with clear goals， ethical principles， and practical strategies. Included and beyond this guidance document， our collective work will produce additional resources—such as best practice guides， real-world use cases， and professional development tools—to support teachers， administrators， families， and technology partners. By prioritizing transparency， data protection， and access， we help ensure that AI’s integration in Florida classrooms enhances teaching and learning， empowers students for success， and advances the mission of a world-class education system. We welcome feedback and consider the Guidance a flexible， iterative document. Guiding Principles The FL K-12 AI Task Force encourages stakeholders to approach AI in education by utilizing the following principles: Cultivate AI Literacy and Understanding Establish a foundation of broad AI literacy (awareness about AI) for all K-12 learners， ensuring they understand the presence and implications of AI in their daily lives. Prioritize Ethical and Responsible AI Integration Ensure AI education includes dedicated， ethics and fairness-focused experiences that address related issues of ethics， impacts， and careers. Guide all stakeholders in the evaluation of AI systems， focusing on responsible use and the societal implications of these emerging technologies. Empower and Prepare Educators Support the co-design with teachers and teacher preparation programs to ensure educators are fully equipped with the content knowledge and instructional strategies necessary to implement AI standards effectively and with confidence. Support School & District Administrators and IT Professionals Cultivate an ongoing professional learning community and network for school district administrators and IT professionals to exchange policies， discuss successes and challenges， and learn from the unique Florida educational ecosystem. Support Flexible Curriculum Integration and Pedagogical Excellence Provide models for integrating AI learning into/with other subjects to demonstrate its interdisciplinary nature. Examine and recommend a wide range of and effective pedagogies (e.g.， unplugged activities， creation of artifacts， project-based learning， embodied cognition) appropriate for developing an understanding about AI across all grade bands. Intended Audiences This document is for:  To guide in-service and pre-service teachers in using AI implementation effectively in and for the classroom.  To help learners understand responsible use of AI–its benefits， opportunities， and concerns– so that they are prepared for an AI-enhanced future.  To keep families informed about how AI is used in schools and what safety measures are in place.  To support decision-makers in planning and managing AI integration in schools.  To provide technical guidance on procurement， implementation and maintenance of AI systems responsibly. Download How AI Mode Works (opens in a new tab) Foundations What is AI? AI is not one thing. It is a collection of technologies that can recognize patterns， generate content， classify information， summarize sources， and support decisions when used with human review. Artificial intelligence Computer systems designed to perform tasks that usually require human intelligence， such as language， perception， planning， or prediction. Machine learning A method where systems learn patterns from data instead of following only hand-written rules. Large language models AI models trained on language patterns to predict and generate text， summaries， explanations， and other outputs. Starting point The value of AI depends on the instructional， privacy， and governance systems around it. AI is... A tool to enhance human capability. A support for operations and learning when used within district guardrails. A reality of the modern workforce that students and staff must learn to evaluate. AI is not... A replacement for human critical thinking. A replacement for staff review and accountability. An autonomous decision-maker for grading， discipline， services， or personnel matters. Personalized tutoring， adaptive problem sequencing， dyslexia reading support， hybrid GenAI-adaptive programming feedback， and structured teacher assistance show credible gains. Risk Do not use AI detection or scoring as unchecked authority. Detection tools and LLM scoring systems can align with humans in aggregate while still shifting criteria， compressing scores， and disadvantaging learner groups. Tool adoption Replace vendor-led adoption with executable governance. Districts need approval pathways， privacy review， classroom-use guidance， audit routines， staff training， and model checks that evolve as tools change. Learning design Protect the thinking students must still do. AI can reduce barriers， but unrestricted chatbot access can also create cognitive offloading， dependence， surface fluency， and a false sense of learning. Our approach The Artificial Intelligence Leadership Framework Broward's own AILF replaces the generic industry principles previously shown here. It is a district-wide guide for leaders to use AI responsibly， ethically， and strategically， grounded in the Florida Educational Leadership Standards (FELS 1 through 8) and aligned with the district's Strategic Plan. ”Leading ethical， strategic AI integration to advance student success and excellence.” The AILF is not a mandate to use AI tools， nor does it replace district policy， professional judgment， or evaluation frameworks. It outlines effective leadership practices for using AI purposefully to support teaching， learning， and organizational effectiveness. AILF 1 AI for Ethical and Responsible Leadership FELS 1， Professional and Ethical Norms Leadership focus: Leaders shall ensure that all AI use is ethical， responsible， and aligned with professional norms to promote the academic success and well-being of all students. Safeguards: protect student and staff data privacy in all AI applications; identify and mitigate potential bias in AI tools and outputs; establish clear guidelines for responsible AI use; promote equitable access to AI resources and opportunities. AILF 2 AI for Vision， Strategy， and Change Management FELS 2， Vision and Mission Leadership focus: Leaders shall establish， communicate， and sustain a shared vision for the strategic and ethical use of AI， aligned with the school and district mission， instructional priorities， and goals for student success. Safeguards: support development and communication of AI expectations aligned to the School Improvement Plan and district strategic priorities; involve staff， students， and stakeholders; enhance teaching， learning， and student outcomes; monitor progress toward defined AI integration goals. AILF 3 AI for Organizational Management FELS 3， School Operations， Management， and Safety Leadership focus: Leaders shall leverage AI to strengthen organizational systems， increase operational efficiency， and support strategic decision-making aligned to a safe school environment， supervision， emergency procedures， and student and staff well-being. Safeguards: improve scheduling， communication， and resource allocation; integrate AI insights into school improvement planning and data review; streamline operational tasks to maximize time for instructional leadership; identify inefficiencies and data-informed improvements. AILF 4 AI for Student Learning and Continuous School Improvement FELS 4 Leadership focus: Leaders shall strategically utilize AI to enhance data-informed decision-making， strengthen intervention systems， and improve measurable student outcomes for all student groups. Safeguards: systematically analyze student performance， subgroup， and longitudinal data; inform intervention design and progress monitoring; conduct data analysis aligned to School Improvement Plan goals; support equitable access to rigorous learning for all students. AILF 5 AI for Inclusive and Supportive Learning Environments FELS 5， Learning Environment Leadership focus: Leaders shall ensure that AI is used to cultivate a caring， inclusive， rigorous， and supportive learning environment that promotes student belonging， engagement， well-being， safety， and academic success for all students. Safeguards: promote a positive， inclusive， student-centered culture; reinforce high expectations for behavior and engagement; monitor environments for rigor， safety， and respect; support staff in addressing social， emotional， behavioral， and academic needs. AILF 6 AI for Capacity Building and Talent Development FELS 6， Recruitment and Professional Learning Leadership focus: Leaders shall ensure that AI is strategically used to strengthen recruitment， professional learning， instructional coaching， and staff support systems that build the capacity of instructional personnel to improve teaching， learning， and student outcomes. Safeguards: differentiate professional learning based on teacher needs and experience; design job-embedded learning aligned to school goals; strengthen instructional coaching cycles; support recruitment， onboarding， and retention systems. AILF 7 AI for Leadership and Innovation FELS 7， Building Leadership Expertise Leadership focus: Leaders shall ensure that AI is strategically used to strengthen leadership expertise， distributed leadership structures， succession planning， and organizational leadership capacity to support long-term school improvement and sustainability. Safeguards: strengthen distributed leadership and clarify responsibilities; support assistant principal， coach， and teacher-leader growth; support succession planning and leadership continuity; analyze leadership challenges through multiple lenses. AILF 8 AI for Communication and Partnerships FELS 8， Meaningful Parent， Family and Community Engagement Leadership focus: Leaders shall ensure that AI is used to strengthen reciprocal communication， build trusting relationships， and promote meaningful collaboration with families and the community to support student success and well-being. Safeguards: communicate clearly， consistently， and respectfully with families; differentiate communication to meet diverse family needs; analyze stakeholder feedback to inform decisions; establish systems for two-way communication and ongoing collaboration. Human leadership， always Across all eight domains， the AILF is explicit that AI tools， including Microsoft Copilot， are meant to enhance， not replace， human leadership， professional expertise， ethical judgment， and student-centered decision-making. Final decisions remain human. What is Artificial Intelligence? Artificial Intelligence， often called AI， is technology that can help people organize information， identify patterns， generate ideas， draft content， provide feedback， and support learning activities. Artificial Intelligence is a tool used to support teachers and students. It does not replace the educational relationship among teachers， students， and families. Teachers remain central to learning. 2. Why is the district talking about Artificial Intelligence? Artificial Intelligence is already part of daily life， the workplace， and future career pathways. Broward County Public Schools wants students to understand these tools and learn to use them safely， responsibly， ethically， and with adult guidance. 3. What does “Human Intelligence First， Artificial Intelligence Second” mean? It means people remain the decision makers. Teachers lead instruction. Students do the thinking. Families remain partners. Artificial Intelligence can support learning， but it should never replace human judgment， relationships， creativity， care， or responsibility. 4. Will Artificial Intelligence replace teachers? No. Teachers remain at the center of learning. Teachers make instructional decisions， build relationships， provide feedback， support students， and determine how tools are used in the classroom. 5. Are elementary students using district-approved Artificial Intelligence tools? No. Broward County Public Schools does not currently use or provide district-approved， student-facing Artificial Intelligence tools to students in kindergarten through grade 5. Because students may still encounter public tools outside district-controlled settings， families should talk with their children about safe and responsible use. 6. Will elementary students learn about Artificial Intelligence? Elementary students may receive age-appropriate instruction about Artificial Intelligence literacy and digital citizenship， such as how technology can generate information， why information must be checked， and how to use technology safely. The specific curriculum and timing are still being reviewed. This instruction does not mean elementary students are given access to district-approved student-facing Artificial Intelligence tools. Because students may still encounter public tools outside district-controlled settings， families should talk with their children about safe and responsible use. 7. What is the difference between teacher-facing and student-facing tools? Teacher-facing tools help educators with tasks such as planning， creating resources， communicating， and differentiating instruction. Student-facing tools are tools students may interact with directly， but only in approved settings， with teacher direction and monitoring. 8. Are teachers required to use district Artificial Intelligence tools? No. Based on current district practice， teachers’ use of district Artificial Intelligence tools is optional. Use must follow district guidance， completion of required training， have instructional purpose， and be guided by the teacher’s professional judgment. 9. How are teachers trained? Teachers receive training and support through a variety of formats， including online， blended， and in-person sessions， as well as learning communities and coaching. These opportunities address numerous content areas and support teacher growth and development. Specific to Artificial Intelligence， current and planned training includes responsible use， ethics， privacy， instructional best practices， human oversight， and guidance on when Artificial Intelligence should and should not be used. 10. What is Khanmigo? Khanmigo is an Artificial Intelligence-supported tutoring and guidance tool through Khan Academy. It prompts students to think through problems instead of simply providing answers. It supports student thinking through guiding prompts， while teachers remain responsible for directing its instructional use. Khanmigo acts like a tutor and cannot be used as a shortcut to get answers. 11. What is HMH Writable or Revision Aid? HMH Writable， including Revision Aid， supports writing and revision. It can provide feedback while students are drafting so they can revise before submitting work to the teacher. It is not a conversational Artificial Intelligence tool， and it does not replace the teacher’s review or feedback. 12. What is MagicSchool? MagicSchool is an Artificial Intelligence platform designed primarily to support teachers with planning， instructional resources， differentiation， communication， and efficiency. MagicSchool is teacher-facing. 13. What is MagicStudent? MagicStudent is MagicSchool’s student-facing Artificial Intelligence platform. It is designed to help students practice skills and receive real-time feedback under direct teacher supervision. MagicStudent is not currently available for Broward County Public Schools students. 14. Will there be additional training if MagicStudent is used in schools? Yes. If MagicStudent is approved for future student use， teachers will be required to complete additional training before turning on student-facing features. The training requirements， content， and procedures will be finalized before any student access is granted or shared in the classroom. 15. Will families be notified if a teacher uses MagicStudent with their child? Yes. If the district approves MagicStudent for future student use， families will be informed before implementation. Communication procedures， parent information， and any available choices will be shared after related policy and procedures are finalized. For the latest updates please visit browardschools.ai . 16. Do Broward County Public Schools approved tools create content for students? Approved student tools are to be used to coach， guide， and support students. Tools are not to replace student thinking， creativity， or create completed work for students to submit as their own. 17. Will Artificial Intelligence be used for grading? Broward County Public Schools does not use Artificial Intelligence in place of a teacher to assign a final grade. An approved tool may assist with the teacher’s review， suggest follow-up instruction to strengthen student skills， and provide feedback during learning; however， the teacher remains responsible for reviewing student work， giving final feedback， and determining grades. 18. How are Artificial Intelligence tools selected and approved? District-approved tools are reviewed for instructional value， privacy， safety， accessibility， age appropriateness， teacher training needs， responsible use， and alignment with district goals. 19. What are real-time threat detection and real-time moderation? Real-time threat detection means a tool can alert adults quickly if a student interaction includes serious concerns such as self-harm or threats to others. Real-time moderation means the tool redirects or stops conversations that move into unsafe， inappropriate， or overly personal areas. 20. Who receives student safety alerts? For approved student-facing tools， teachers receive alerts when a serious threat is detected. Depending on the level of concern， the alert may also be escalated to administrators and other trained personnel. 21. How is student information protected? The district reviews approved tools for privacy and security requirements. Relevant protections include the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)， the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA)， and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA). Florida protects K-12 student data through the Student Online Personal Information Protection Act (Florida SOPIPA)， State Board of Education Rule 6A-1.09550， and the Florida Information Protection Act (FIPA). Student information in approved tools stays within the Broward County Public Schools environment and is not used to train Artificial Intelligence. 22. Do student interactions train the Artificial Intelligence models? No. Under current district requirements， approved Broward County Public Schools tools must not use our students’ interactions to train Artificial Intelligence models. 23. Are ChatGPT， Google AI， or other open tools used? Open public tools such as ChatGPT and Google Artificial Intelligence features are not approved by Broward County Public Schools as student-facing instructional tools. They may still be accessible outside district-controlled settings. The district is reviewing controls for open public tools on school-issued devices， including devices used on home networks. Access may be more difficult to control when students use devices on home networks. Families are encouraged to remind students to use only teacher-directed， district-approved tools for schoolwork and to discuss safe， responsible technology use at home. 24. Can families preview or test approved tools? Yes， preview and testing opportunities are being planned. The district is exploring possible regional sessions where parents and guardians could see or interact with tools that may be used in the future. Details have not yet been finalized and will be made available when they are. Latest updates are available at browardschools.ai . 25. Will Artificial Intelligence increase screen time? The district recognizes family concerns about screen time. Artificial Intelligence is a tool， and use must have a clear learning purpose and should be balanced with reading， writing， discussion， collaboration， hands-on learning， movement， and direct interaction with teachers and classmates. Specific requirements continue to be refined and guided by data， policy， and instructional guidance. 26. How is Artificial Intelligence different from i-Ready and other education technology? Artificial Intelligence is one type of educational technology. i-Ready is not an Artificial Intelligence tool. Families often connect these tools because they involve devices， screen time， homework， and classroom use. The district acknowledges concerns with screen time and student overdependence on technology and continues to listen to and address the concerns by constantly and regularly reviewing feedback， student data， appropriate use， and impact on student learning. 27. How will Artificial Intelligence support reading， writing， and social skills? Artificial Intelligence can support reading and writing by providing feedback， helping teachers differentiate instruction， or presenting ideas in different ways. It is a tool that helps inform instruction; it does not replace discussion， human interaction， social development， or teacher guidance. The district’s position is that Artificial Intelligence should never replace human interaction. 28. Could Artificial Intelligence reduce critical thinking or creativity? This is a valid concern. Students still need to read， write， solve problems， think independently， communicate clearly， and create original ideas. Our approach is for Artificial Intelligence to support and develop these skills， not to replace them， by teaching students to use Artificial Intelligence responsibly and ethically. Teachers remain central to instruction and responsible for setting expectations， guiding， and reviewing student work. 29. Will students be taught about the risks and limits of Artificial Intelligence? Yes. The district is committed to responsible use. As part of our Artificial Intelligence vision， instruction will help students understand both how to use Artificial Intelligence and when not to use it. This includes checking accuracy， avoiding overreliance， protecting privacy， using tools ethically， and verifying generated information. 30. How does Artificial Intelligence help teachers without replacing them? Artificial Intelligence is a tool that will help teachers save time with planning， resource creation， differentiation， communication， and administrative tasks. It will be used to support educators， not replace them. Teachers remain responsible for， and central to， individualized instruction， feedback， relationships， and decisions about student learning. 31. How will success be measured? The district plans to review success through multiple measures， including usage， student outcomes， student engagement， teacher workload， teacher time saved， and whether tools support and enhance individualized student instruction. Data will be shared in district monthly reports to the School Board and public updates through Broward Powered by AI. Latest updates are available at browardschools.ai . 32. What would cause the district to stop using a tool? Every instructional tool is evaluated on an ongoing basis. This applies to traditional and digital tools， including Artificial Intelligence tools. If evidence and data show that a tool does not support district goals， improve learning， protect students， or meet safety and privacy requirements， the district reconsiders， adjusts， replaces， suspends， or discontinues its use. 33. Are there costs for the district to use Khanmigo， Writable， or MagicSchool? These tools do not currently cost the district additional funds to use. Khanmigo is through Khan Academy， Writable is connected to the adopted instructional materials， and MagicSchool was donated. Teacher training is provided through district staff， vendor-provided training， or agreements and does not cost the district， schools， or teachers extra. Long-term costs and value continue to be reviewed and assessed to ensure they meet district student learning goals. 34. How does Artificial Intelligence affect the district’s climate goals? We are all concerned about the energy and environmental impact AI can have. The use of Artificial Intelligence can help us better track and improve the use of operational systems， such as lighting， heating， ventilation， air conditioning， and building systems， to help reduce energy use. Environmental impact remains an important question that we will continue reviewing. 35. How can families stay informed? Before continuing or expanding a tool， the district reviews its educational value， student outcomes， total cost， available funding sources， and whether the tool is producing the expected results. 46. Are there additional requirements connected to the MagicSchool donation through the Community Foundation of Broward? MagicSchool is supported through a donation. At this time， the district can provide only quantitative data because MagicSchool and MagicStudent have not yet been fully rolled out. As additional data becomes available， the district will share findings with funders and the community by posting reports on the Broward Powered by AI website: browardschools.ai . 47. How many schools currently use Prisms Virtual Reality? Prisms Virtual Reality is an approved， teacher-directed immersive math and science tool. The number of participating schools at this time is 58 total schools， including all schools with middle grades (K-8 and 6-12 combinations) plus a small number of high schools and centers. 48. Do students use their own district login when accessing approved Artificial Intelligence tools? Approved tools are made available through the student access portal， known as Clever. Students can access only the tools available for their grade level and instructional setting. Some features must also be assigned or enabled by a teacher. 49. Is a student’s work in MagicStudent private? MagicStudent is not currently available to Broward County Public Schools students. Information entered into approved tools stays within the district environment and is not used to train Artificial Intelligence models. Approved tools allow authorized teachers or administrators to review student activity for instruction， safety， and appropriate use. 50. Are students’ Individualized Education Programs (IEP) entered into MagicSchool? At this time， details from a student’s Individualized Education Program are not automatically loaded into MagicSchool. The district currently has this feature turned off. The district team is reviewing features and processes to ensure that， if activated， the feature will align with district and state standards and follow Broward County Public Schools privacy requirements. 51. Does district approval of Artificial Intelligence change the rules for using Teachers Pay Teachers resources? Teachers Pay Teachers is an online marketplace where prekindergarten through grade 12 educators buy， sell， and share educational resources. These resources may not align with Florida standards or district requirements. By comparison， Artificial Intelligence tools approved and implemented by Broward County Public Schools are vetted and reviewed for effectiveness， safety， and alignment with Florida state standards. 52. Are schools or employees rewarded for using Artificial Intelligence tools? Artificial Intelligence tools such as MagicSchool are optional supports for teachers. Their use is based on a clear instructional or operational purpose， not on earning a reward. Microsoft is supporting the district’s effort to improve operations and productivity by offering an incentive to encourage the use of Copilot. The incentive is awarded to the school with the highest use， and the funds go directly to that school to support its needs. 53. Can a teacher set limits or parameters when students use Khanmigo? Khanmigo guides students step by step rather than simply providing answers. Teachers determine how it is used， assign activities or features， and establish classroom expectations for when and how students may use it. Teachers can also enable Focus Mode， a feature that allows teachers to disable Khanmigo for the entire class or individual students for up to four hours at a time. 54. How will the district respond if state law requires parent permission before students use Artificial Intelligence? The district will follow any final legal and policy requirements. The Broward Powered by AI site is intended to provide parent notices， available choices， contacts， and updates. Because requirements may change， families will receive clear information before any student-facing Artificial Intelligence tool is introduced. To stay up to date， please visit browardschools.ai . 55. Is Microsoft Copilot used by students in the classroom? No. Microsoft Copilot Premium is primarily a staff-facing tool and is not available to the general Broward County Public Schools student population. A small group of approved high school students in a specific technology pathway uses a monitored version under staff supervision. 56. Can students open approved Artificial Intelligence programs on their own， such as HMH Writable? Access depends on the tool. Khanmigo is available to eligible secondary students through the district environment. Teachers determine when HMH Writable is assigned or enabled for student work. MagicStudent is not currently available. Student-facing tools and their use remain connected to grade level， instruction， teacher oversight， and district approval. 57. How will the district prevent students from being unfairly accused of using Artificial Intelligence? A student should not be judged only by an automated detector or by how polished the work appears. Teachers should review the student’s process， drafts， sources， assignment expectations， and explanation of the work before reaching a conclusion. The district’s guiding approach keeps human judgment and fair educational decisions at the center. The district also has a task force reviewing procedures to help ensure that tools used to identify copied or Artificial Intelligence-authored work are used appropriately， include safeguards， and have proper oversight. 58. How will Artificial Intelligence tools support students with disabilities and other individual learning needs? Accessibility is one of the district’s tool-selection principles. Artificial Intelligence may help teachers adjust reading levels， provide different ways to access content， and create more individualized support. Approved tools must pass an accessibility review， and they do not replace a student’s Individualized Education Program， Section 504 plan， accommodations， specialized instruction， or support from educators and service providers. The Exceptional Student Education & Support Services Department is involved in reviewing tools to help ensure that district standards are properly incorporated into any tool released for teacher use. 59. Does using more Artificial Intelligence conflict with the district’s goal of reducing screen time? These goals do not have to conflict when technology is used for a clear， limited learning purpose. The district recognizes concerns about total screen time. Artificial Intelligence supports instruction; it does not replace reading， writing， discussion， movement， hands-on learning， or interaction between teachers and students. The district strives for a balanced approach to student learning and the use of technology， and continues to monitor and review its use， adjusting based on data and input from parents and teachers. 60. Do approved Artificial Intelligence tools allow adults to review what students enter， and who can see it? Approved student-facing tools include monitoring， moderation， and flagging features. Teachers oversee student use， and safety concerns are shared with appropriate school administrators. The exact level of visibility depends on the tool and the educational or safety purpose. Student information is protected， remains within the district environment， and is shared only with authorized staff who need it. 61. Can parents review their child’s prompts and work in approved Artificial Intelligence tools? As with other student work， parents may ask the teacher or school to explain how a tool is being used and may ask questions about their child’s work. 62. Will parents need to give permission before schools use Artificial Intelligence with their child? The district will follow final state law， School Board policy， and district procedures. Current family resources are designed to provide notice， available choices， contacts， and updates. Because requirements may change， families will receive clear information before a student-facing tool is introduced. To stay up to date， please visit browardschools.ai . 63. Who trains the Artificial Intelligence systems used by Broward County Public Schools? Artificial Intelligence models are developed and trained by vendors using large data sets before the district approves them. Broward County Public Schools reviews tools for privacy， safety， accessibility， reliability， and instructional value. District-approved tools do not use Broward County Public Schools students or their data to train Artificial Intelligence models. 64. How does a teacher provide feedback when students use HMH Writable? Teachers can add an assignment rubric for students to use while writing. HMH Writable can provide color-coded suggestions on grammar， structure， word choice， and alignment with the rubric before the student submits the work. The tool provides an additional layer of support， but the teacher still reviews the work and provides final feedback， whether during class， after the student submits the work， or both. 65. Can students use Khanmigo when they need tutoring help? Yes. All students in grades 6 through 8 currently have access to Khanmigo， and students in grades 9 through 12 have access through the Florida Tutoring Advantage Grant. Khanmigo provides step-by-step guidance， study strategies， and links to Khan Academy practice. Teachers may also assign additional activities or enable additional features. 66. When students use MagicStudent or another approved Artificial Intelligence tool， will it check whether their answers are accurate? The way a tool responds depends on the tool and the activity selected by the teacher. MagicStudent is designed to guide students through their thinking by asking questions and providing prompts instead of giving them an answer. It can help a student reconsider an answer or think through the next step， but it does not replace the teacher’s review or judgment. Teachers determine the learning goal and how the tool should support the activity. 67. Will MagicStudent grade student work? No. MagicStudent is intended to coach and guide students， not independently grade their work. A teacher remains responsible for reviewing student work， providing feedback， and making grading decisions. 68. How does MagicStudent support students without doing the thinking for them? MagicStudent uses a question-based approach similar to tutoring. It may ask follow-up questions， prompt students to explain their thinking， or guide them toward information they should consider. The goal is to support the student’s reasoning rather than create the work or provide the final answer. 69. Can teachers decide what MagicStudent should focus on during an activity? Yes. Teachers have the ability to define the purpose of the activity and the type of thinking students should practice. This is important because accuracy may not be the goal in every assignment; for example， some activities may focus on building an argument， practicing creativity， developing fluency， or explaining reasoning. The teacher remains responsible for setting the expectations and deciding how the tool supports student learning. 70. Can Artificial Intelligence support teacher planning without creating the lesson for the teacher? Yes. An Artificial Intelligence tool can be set up to coach a teacher through the planning process by asking questions about the lesson， student needs， learning goals， and instructional decisions. This approach supports the teacher’s thinking instead of replacing it or automatically creating a lesson plan without teacher input. 71. Will students learn how Artificial Intelligence works， including generative Artificial Intelligence and Artificial Intelligence agents， rather than only learning how to use it as a productivity tool? Yes. Artificial Intelligence literacy is an important part of the district’s approach. In elementary school， students learn the ideas behind how Artificial Intelligence works without using student-facing Artificial Intelligence tools. Through age-appropriate activities， students learn about patterns， data， predictions， checking information， privacy， fairness， and how technology can help solve problems. As students grow， this foundation prepares them to understand more advanced ideas and to use approved tools thoughtfully and responsibly. The goal is not simply to teach students how to use a tool; it is to help them understand how the technology works， what it can and cannot do， and why human judgment remains essential. 72. How will the district help students and teachers understand that Artificial Intelligence is a tool， not a person that thinks or knows things the way people do? The district’s Artificial Intelligence literacy message is clear: Artificial Intelligence is a tool， not a person. It looks for patterns in information and may use those patterns to make a prediction or suggestion. It can be useful and still be wrong. Elementary lessons build this understanding through age-appropriate activities that focus on patterns， data， predictions， and checking answers rather than using student-facing Artificial Intelligence tools. For secondary students， approved tools are used in teacher-guided settings， and teachers and students are expected to review results， question the information， and make the final decisions. Human thinking， evidence， and responsibility remain most important. 73. How will students learn to recognize when an Artificial Intelligence tool agrees with or flatters the user instead of providing accurate information? Students need to understand that a confident， friendly， or agreeable response is not always a correct response. The district’s Artificial Intelligence literacy approach teaches students to question technology， check information， and use reliable sources before accepting or sharing an answer. Families can reinforce this thinking by asking， “Could the computer be wrong?”， “What information did it use?”， and “How can we check the answer?” Students should compare the response with trusted evidence， consider whether important viewpoints are missing， and ask an adult or teacher when they are unsure. The goal is to help students use Artificial Intelligence thoughtfully without treating agreement as proof that an answer is accurate. 74. How does Broward County Public Schools help ensure that Artificial Intelligence image-generation tools are safe for students? Broward County Public Schools reviews Artificial Intelligence tools for safety and educational value before student use. Image generation features are not automatically available to students and must be turned on by a teacher for a specific classroom activity. MagicSchool’s image tool uses Adobe Express and includes a more restrictive， G-rated content filter designed to help prevent inappropriate content from being generated. As with all district-approved Artificial Intelligence tools， human oversight， transparency， privacy， and age-appropriate use remain essential expectations. Myths vs. facts Myth Artificial Intelligence will replace teachers. Fact Teachers remain central to learning and decision making in Broward County Public Schools. Myth Elementary students are currently using district-approved Artificial Intelligence tools. Fact No district-approved student-facing Artificial Intelligence tools are currently available for elementary students in kindergarten through grade 5. Myth Artificial Intelligence will make human relationships less important. Fact Broward County Public Schools believes human connection and relationships are essential to student learning and development. Myth Students have unrestricted access to district Artificial Intelligence tools. Fact Under current district practice， approved student use is grade-based， teacher directed， teacher monitored， and limited to supported instructional settings. Because students may still encounter public tools outside district-controlled settings， families should talk with their children about safe and responsible use. Myth MagicStudent is currently open for Broward County Public Schools students. Fact MagicStudent is not currently available to Broward County Public Schools students. If it is approved in the future， notifications will be shared with families and trained teachers will direct and monitor its use under district oversight. Myth Artificial Intelligence will grade students without teacher input. Fact Broward County Public Schools does not use Artificial Intelligence in place of a teacher to assign a final grade. Artificial Intelligence may help support feedback. Teachers remain responsible for review， feedback， and grading decisions. Myth Student data is used to train district-approved Artificial Intelligence tools. Fact Under current district requirements， student information in approved tools must remain within the Broward County Public Schools environment and cannot be used to train Artificial Intelligence models. Myth The district is relying only on vendors to decide whether tools are safe. Fact The district reviews student-facing tools for instructional value， privacy， safety， and other requirements， and performs its own rigorous vetting process， including adversarial prompting， real-time threat detection， and real-time moderation for student-facing tools. Myth Artificial Intelligence automatically means more screen time. Fact The district supports balanced， purposeful， and developmentally appropriate technology use. Artificial Intelligence use must have a clear learning purpose and should not replace direct instruction， human interaction， or hands-on learning. Myth Families do not have a way to stay involved. Board action BCPS Adopts New AI Policy that Puts Teachers and Parents in the Driver’s Seat The School Board of Broward County adopted a new Artificial Intelligence Policy at its September 15th meeting. The policy is a culmination of a year-long process that included input from teachers， parents， students， and community members. It ensures AI is used responsibly and ethically， with guardrails in place to protect student and staff data， and includes provisions to ensure teachers control how AI is used in their classrooms and that parents are informed and given agency in how their children learn and use AI. Of particular note is the guarantee that all student-facing generative AI tools need to provide real-time threat detection， escalation， and moderation， which is one of the highest bars set for student generative AI use in the country.
