Children’s Internet Protection Act 47 U.S.C. § 254 34 C.F.R. 54.520 Acceptable Use and CIPA Compliance All Students and employees shall comply with the District’s Policy on the Acceptable Use of District Technology when using AI tools on school district technology. Violations of the District’s Acceptable Use Policy may result in disciplinary action against the student or employee. Student use of AI tools while using District technology or engaged in District activities is also governed by the Student Code of Conduct， which is hereby incorporated by reference. All AI tools used by the district will be CIPA compliant. Grading Student Work Approved AI websites and applications may be used to assist with the grading of student work product， but final decisions on assignment grades shall be determined by teachers and not solely by AI technology. Teachers shall ensure that personally identifiable student records are kept secure when using any such grading technology. AI Use in Operations The Superintendent or designee shall establish protocols to verify the accuracy and reliability of the output from AI tools prior to the use of such tools for budgeting， payroll， financial or population forecasting， HR analytics， and similar operational tasks. While AI tools may be used to assist in HR processes so long as the protocols above are in place， the board directs that final decision-making regarding employee evaluations， promotions， and hiring be human decisions and not solely by AI technology to ensure fairness， equity， and compliance with anti-discrimination laws. Professional Development The board directs the Superintendent or designee to provide regular professional development training for administrators， teachers， and staff on the ethical and appropriate use of AI in school. Retrieved from https://tacc.utexas.edu/education/educators/align/. 1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly become integral in daily life， and Texas K-12 students and educators are navigating the opportunities and risks largely on their own. The Texas AI in Education Task Force， a coalition of educators， administrators， higher education professionals， industry leaders， parents， and nonprofit representatives， convened by the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) at The University of Texas at Austin， produced this report to offer state policymakers a clear-eyed assessment of where Texas stands and a concrete path forward. THE CHALLENGE Texas is one of only five states with no formal AI guidance for K-12 education， even though student use has skyrocketed. Currently， only about a quarter of Texas school districts pro- vide guidance for AI use for either teachers or students. This leaves students without the guardrails needed to help them navigate AI appropriately. Continued inaction risks student misuse， over-reliance on AI， harm to cognitive and social-emotional development， data privacy violations， workforce unpreparedness， and uneven educational experiences across 1，200+ districts. This is particularly serious given the ubiquitous access to AI that today’s students have outside of school. Because Texas is one of the largest public school systems in the country， with roughly 1 in 10 U.S. K-12 students and 1 in 9 U.S. public school teachers， this indecision has an outsized impact on student preparation for the entire country. THE STAKES The safety of Texas’ students is paramount and our children are exposed to AI embedded in the technology they use every day in and out of the classroom. We need guidelines， literacy frameworks， and professional preparation to support the responsible implementation of AI. With 5.5 million K-12 students whose futures depend on navigating an AI-driven world， the Task Force calls on state leaders to act with urgency. The infrastructure exists; what is needed now is the political will and investment to use it. THE FOUR RECOMMENDATIONS 1. Establish State Leadership Texas should designate a leader with the authority to coordinate a statewide K-12 AI strategy and convene an advisory board of educators， parents， industry representatives， and policymakers. Without central accountability， the state’s response will remain fragmented across 1，200+ independent districts. 2. Issue Statewide Guidance Texas should publish guidance covering responsible use policies for both educators and students， data privacy， AI procurement and student assessment. Guidance should also reflect the need for community and family engagement in the creation and implementation of local policies. 3. Fund Professional Development The state should invest in a coordinated， hub-and-spoke initiative to build AI literacy across all educators and administrators. The existing Texas Computer Science Pipeline network should be expanded to address AI safety， responsible use， and instructional integration as appropriate， while building long-term capacity in educator preparation programs. 4. Update Student Learning Standards. Texas should incorporate AI literacy through a phased approach of updating the Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS). 2 Introduction AI in Education Task Force Vision: All Texas students are prepared to thrive personally and professionally in an AI-partnered world. Do I have to use Microsoft Copilot Chat， Google Gemini， or ChatGPT Edu? Can I use generative AI Chatbots that I’ve paid for myself to support my work? We highly recommend our staff not use consumer chatbots for work-related activities. Sensitive data is not protected in a way that complies with FERPA policy. For example， if you uploaded a data file into your personal ChatGPT for analysis that includes student ID numbers and names， you have now violated HISD Data privacy policies. Microsoft Copilot Chat， Google Gemini， and ChatGPT Edu reside within the HISD domain and protects sensitive data. We trust that our employees will use their best efforts to access the enterprise-level generative AI tools to support their efficiency and productivity in a way that keeps district data private and secure. Can I use generative AI tools outside of the approved list with my students? We hope our staff continue to explore generative AI tools. And， we also know that we must take great care and responsibility to put vetted products in front of our students. We highly recommend teachers allow only students to use district approved AI tools， such as the preferred Google Gemini or Microsoft Copilot Chat， if they are above the 8th grade or above and have parent permission. Even with vetted tools， teachers must review images for appropriateness and accuracy before showing them to students. For example， a teacher might ask a generative AI image creation tool to show a picture of what a revolutionary war hospital might have looked like. Before embedding it into a lesson， the teacher is responsible for checking the image for accuracy and suitability for the students. Who can I talk to if an issue arises on my campus or in my department concerning a generative AI tool? It is our expectation that campus and central office staff will communicate openly about experiences with generative AI tools. This landscape is new and consistently evolving. If you run into a concerning situation， whereby the generative AI chatbot hallucinates or shares concerning or inaccurate content， it is important to share that information with the AI Support Team. Instructions for how to connect with that team can be found on page 19. How is AI used in Houston ISD， and is it considered a system of record? AI tools in Houston ISD are not systems of record and function only as professional planning and drafting environments. All AI-assisted work is pre-decisional， requires human review， and any finalized or official materials must be stored in HISD-approved systems (e.g.， email， SharePoint， OneDrive， SIS， ERP). AI Guidebook // Frequently Asked Questions 21 Houston Independent School District Frequently Asked Questions Families Are generative AI tools appropriate for my child， especially if they are 8th grade or above? Generative AI tools have different age restrictions. At this time， Houston ISD will provide access to Google Gemini to students， 8th grade and above who have obtained parental consent. The district will prioritize responsible use training for both students and staff as well as support students if content is returned that is inappropriate. Is my student’s data protected while using generative AI tools? Student data protection is a top priority in Houston ISD. If a student uses consumer-based AI tools (such as public versions of ChatGPT) outside of district-managed platforms， any information entered may be shared with the company that operates the tool. Houston ISD provides access to secure， district-managed AI environments， including the enterprise version of Google Gemini for staff and students ages 13 and older. These tools do not use student or staff data to train external AI models and operate within HISD’s security and privacy requirements， including access controls， monitoring， and safeguards designed to prevent the exposure or misuse of sensitive information. What if I have questions or concerns about how my student engages with generative AI tools? With any new initiative， we expect our families to have questions about how their students might engage with this new technology. A family should feel comfortable in reaching out to their child’s teacher with questions. In addition， families can also submit concerns to the AI Support Team. Instructions for how to connect with that team can be found on page 19. If I do not give my student permission to access generative AI tools， are they able to still engage in learning? Yes. Houston ISD believes AI literacy is an important skill for Destination 2035， and we respect the decisions families make regarding generative AI use. Students without parental consent will continue to receive high-quality， equitable instruction without direct AI tool interaction， including alternative learning opportunities as needed. Teachers may model AI use or provide AI-supported materials that do not require individual student accounts， and no student will be disadvantaged academically or in grading. title: Policy 232.1 - Use of Artificial Intelligence (IDEA Public Schools)
full_text: 232.1 Use of Artificial Intelligence The School is committed to supporting students and staff in the appropriate use of artificial intelligence (“AI”). The use of AI technology is encouraged when used appropriately and ethically. AI may be integrated into academic material responsibly to prepare students for the successful integration of innovative technologies. The School will strive for the implementation of AI to be human-centered and empower students and staff. If utilizing artificial intelligence technology， students and staff shall abide by this policy and all relevant related policies. Definitions Artificial intelligence (AI): A machine-based system that can， for a given set of human-defined objectives， make predictions， recommendations， or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. Artificial intelligence systems use machine- and human-based inputs to perceive real and virtual environments; abstract such perceptions into models through analysis in an automated manner; and use model inference to formulate options for information or action. Generative AI: Any internet-based generative artificial intelligence programs that make use of large language model algorithms to make something new. AI used for auto-complete， minor text predictions， and/or grammar/spelling/punctuation suggestions， commonly found in most word- processing applications， is not considered generative AI. AI tool: AI applications， algorithms， or systems that make use of AI to generate outputs based on human inputs， with an emphasis on generative AI. Data Privacy The School is committed to protecting student and staff data consistent with state and federal laws and regulations. The use of AI shall adhere to existing data privacy policies including， but not limited to， policies related to the release of student records and information (see Policy 294). Procurement of AI Tools The adoption and use of AI tools shall be in accordance with the School’s procurement policies and in alignment with the School’s mission. All AI technologies provided by vendors shall adhere to the School’s policies and current state and federal laws and regulations. Acceptable Use of AI It is understood that all students and staff may use AI technology from time-to-time on School grounds; provided however， AI shall always be used in a manner appropriate to the School’s academic and moral goals， and is only permissible to be used in the academic setting when authorized by the classroom instructor. Failure to use AI technology in an appropriate manner may subject students and staff to disciplinary action. Artificial Intelligence Technology may not be utilized for the following: 1. Violating the conditions of federal and Ohio law dealing with students’ and employees’ rights to privacy; 2. Creating images which may be offensive to another user; bullying， insulting， intimidating， or attacking others; or transmitting any material in violation of federal or state law. 3. Accessing or creating profanity， obscenity， abusive， pornographic， and/ or impolite language or materials; accessing materials in violation of the Student Code of Conduct; or viewing， creating， or accessing materials that you would not want instructors and parents to see. Should a student encounter any inappropriate materials by accident， he/she should report it to his or her instructors immediately. 4. Violating copyright laws by utilizing copyrighted images. All copyright laws must be respected. 5. Plagiarizing works through AI Technology. Plagiarism is taking ideas of others and presenting them as if they were original to the user. While AI Technology may be used to support a student’s learning， AI generated work shall not replace a student’s work. 6. Damaging Technology devices， computers， computer systems， or computer networks (for example， by the creation， introduction， or spreading of computer viruses， physically abusing hardware， altering source codes or software settings， etc.). 7. Using the Technology or the Internet for commercial purposes or activities， which are defined as offering or providing goods or services or purchasing goods or services for personal use， and include， but are not limited to， the following: a. any activity that requires an exchange of money and/or credit card numbers; b. any activity that requires entry into an area of service for which the School will be charged a fee; c. any purchase or sale of any kind; or d. any use for product advertisement or political lobbying. 8. Using AI for any purpose which is illegal or against the School’s policies or contrary to the School’s mission or best interests. R.C. 3301.24; 15 U.S.C. Section 9401 See also Policy 204.16 Cyber Threats; Policy 232 Technology and Internet Acceptable Use; Policy 271 Student Code of Conduct; Policy 294 Student Records and Release of Information; Policy 397.2 Acceptable Uses of the School’s Equipment; 397.3 Unacceptable Uses of the School’s Equipment. CERTIFICATION The Undersigned， being the Board President， hereby certifies that the foregoing represents a true copy of the Board Policy relating to the Use of Artificial Intelligence policy， as originally adopted by the Board on April 20， 2026， which Policy， is in full force and effect and has not been revoked or amended. ___________________________________ dwight young (Apr 23， 2026 08:39:08 EDT) Dwight Young， Board President Apr 23， 2026 ___________________________________ Date 232.1 Artificial Intelligence Final Audit Report 2026-04-23 Created: 2026-04-22 By: Christina Porter (christina.porter@ideapublicschools.org) Status: Signed Transaction ID: CBJCHBCAABAAS7zyaxueApQhSvjJPOEKqomB1YLT3XCD ”232.1 Artificial Intelligence” History Document created by Christina Porter (christina.porter@ideapublicschools.org) 2026-04-22 - 8:57:35 PM GMT Document emailed to dwight@onebloc.org for signature 2026-04-22 - 8:57:54 PM GMT Email viewed by dwight@onebloc.org 2026-04-22 - 8:59:03 PM GMT Signer dwight@onebloc.org entered name at signing as dwight young 2026-04-23 - 12:39:06 PM GMT Document e-signed by dwight young (dwight@onebloc.org) Signature Date: 2026-04-23 - 12:39:08 PM GMT - Time Source: server Agreement completed. 2026-04-23 - 12:39:08 PM GMT

title: Artificial Intelligence (Fort Bend Independent School District)
full_text: Artificial Intelligence Artificial Intelligence， specifically Generative AI (Gen AI)， is a technology tool that can be trained to think and learn like humans. It has the potential to augment teaching and learning by streamlining administrative tasks， calculating data， running simulations， and refining project development as a thought partner. The capabilities of these technologies also necessitate careful guidance to ensure responsible and equitable usage. The primary goal of the guidelines is to inform students， staff， and stakeholders of the responsible and ethical use of Gen AI and its use with other technology tools. Although Gen AI may be able to create， revise， or complete tasks quickly， the amplification of learning is the primary outcome. title: Artificial Intelligence Guidelines - Administrative Regulations (Argyle Independent School District)
full_text: Board CQC (LOCAL) Administrative Regulations ARGYLE ISD ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE GUIDELINES The Texas Education Agency (TEA) does not enforce a single state-mandated policy on student use of artificial intelligence. Instead， the TEA leaves specific AI adoption， guardrails， and student usage rules up to individual local school districts. The Texas Education Agency does use AI directly to automate the scoring of written responses on STAAR tests. Argyle ISD Board Policy CQD (LOCAL) states: Employees and students shall be permitted to explore AI and implement its use in and out of the classroom in accordance with policy and administrative regulations. The use of AI shall only be as a support tool to enhance student outcomes and shall never take the place of teacher and student decision-making. Any use of AI must comply with law， policy， and administrative regulations relating to student and employee privacy and data security. A student shall only use AI tools with teacher permission and shall be expected to produce original work and properly credit sources， including AI tools used in creating the work. Students who use AI tools to deceptively harm， bully， or harass others shall be disciplined in accordance with the Student Code of Conduct and policy. [See EIA(LOCAL)， FFH， FFI， and the FO series] In her Dear Colleague Letter on the use of artificial intelligence in education， Secretary Linda McMahon outlined five principles for the responsible use of AI: education technologies should be educator-led， ethical， accessible， transparent， and protective of student data. These principles provide a strong foundation not only for artificial intelligence but for educational technology more broadly. The accompanying Administrative Regulations for CDQ (LOCAL) outline the technology standards for artificial intelligence (AI) regarding academic integrity and operational use: ACADEMIC INTEGRITY: These regulations outline guidelines and principles for the responsible and ethical use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational settings. Argyle ISD is committed to academic integrity by fostering a culture of originality and creativity and placing a strong emphasis on ethical practices. We recognize the potential of AI tools to enrich and support learning experiences. However， we strictly prohibit the use of AI to commit authorship fraud. Argyle ISD believes in the importance of individual effort， critical thinking， and the responsible use of all technology. Teachers play a crucial role in educating students about the appropriate use of AI tools， including their strengths and weaknesses， to optimize their value in the learning process. Educators will provide guidelines on the sanctionable use of AI in their classroom and on individual assignments. We emphasize the following expectations regarding the use of AI tools in student assignments: 1. Originality: Students must take personal responsibility for the originality and authorship of their work. Assignments should reflect their own thoughts， ideas， and understanding of the subject matter. 2. Citation: When incorporating AI-generated content into their assignments， students must acknowledge its use and accurately cite and attribute the sources. 3. Integrity: Students should adhere to the principles of academic integrity and honesty. Plagiarism， whether facilitated by AI tools or any other means， is strictly prohibited. Artificial intelligence may never replace a student's own thinking or learning. Unauthorized AI use—including using AI during quizzes， tests， or other assessments， or submitting AI-generated work as original work—constitutes academic dishonesty and will be addressed in accordance with the Student Code of Conduct. Consequences may include， but are not limited to， revision of assignments， loss of assignment credit， parental involvement， or other appropriate measures deemed necessary by the school administration. By upholding these guidelines， we commit to fostering a safe， responsible environment that promotes ethical practices and academic integrity， and that prepares the next generation for the challenges and opportunities of AI technology. OPERATIONAL USE: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a tool designed to support learning and productivity—not replace the critical thinking， creativity， and meaningful relationships that define the Argyle ISD learning experience. Our approach to AI will remain thoughtful， age-appropriate， and aligned with our commitment to Hands-On， Minds-On Learning. Employee Use District employees may use AI tools to enhance instructional planning， professional responsibilities， and operational efficiency， while maintaining student privacy and confidentiality and complying with District policy. Employees remain responsible for all instructional decisions， the accuracy of AI-assisted content， and the protection of confidential or personally identifiable student information. Student Use Grades PK–8 ● Students will not use generative AI for classroom assignments， projects， research， or homework. ● Instruction will emphasize foundational skills， critical thinking， problem solving， collaboration， and authentic student work. ● Exception for District-adopted instructional materials: ○ Students may use Argyle ISD's adopted HMH curriculum， which includes Writable， an instructional writing platform that uses AI to provide feedback during the writing process. When used as part of classroom instruction under a teacher's guidance， Writable serves as an instructional support tool to strengthen students' writing and revision skills. Its use within the adopted curriculum is permitted and is not considered student use of generative AI under these procedures. ○ Students may use Argyle ISD's adopted HMH curriculum resource， Amira， an AI-powered reading tutor used for personalized reading intervention. Amira is a resource for supporting student growth. Grades 9–12 ● Students may use Argyle ISD's adopted HMH curriculum， which includes Writable， an instructional writing platform that uses AI to provide feedback during the writing process. ● Students may use generative AI only when specifically authorized by the classroom teacher for an identified instructional purpose. ● When AI is permitted， students must disclose its use， evaluate the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated information， and remain responsible for the originality and quality of all work submitted. Technology Commitments to the Community

title: PSJA ISD AI Guidebook (Pharr-San Juan-Alamo Independent School District)
full_text: PSJA ISD AI Guidebook If you are having trouble viewing the document， you may download the document. TABLE OF CONTENTS Introduction Guiding Principles Privacy and Security Staff AI Expectations Student AI Expectations Academic Integrity Using AI Responsibly: Examples of Misuse References AI CODE OF ETHICS AND MINIMUM STANDARDS: Texas Department of Information Resources. Per Government Code 2054.702， State and local government entities that use AI are required to adopt the code. TAC 219. INTRODUCTION This guidebook supports students， families， and staff in building AI literacy and using GenAI safely， responsibly， and effectively. As AI technologies continue to evolve， this guidebook will be updated to reflect emerging tools， best practices， and changing educational needs. What is AI and GenAI? Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science focused on building machines that mimic human intelligence. It generally falls into two main categories: Predictive (Traditional) AI: Analyzes existing data to recognize patterns， make choices， or predict outcomes. Examples: Movie recommendations， auto-correct， and digital assistants (Siri/Alexa). Generative AI (GenAI): Processes massive datasets to create entirely new， original content. Examples: Generating new text， images， code， or audio (ChatGPT， Gemini). Our Why PSJA ISD's commitment to College³ - Ready. Connected. Complete. calls us to equip every learner with the knowledge， skills， and character needed to thrive in an AI-enabled world. Learners AI serves as a catalyst to enrich instruction， promote equity， and prepare graduates for future-ready success. For Our Educators AI is a tool to increase productivity and elevate professional practice while keeping human connection at the center of the classroom. GUIDING PRINCIPLES Adapted from AI guidance for schools toolkit， by TeachAI， 2025 (https://www.teachai.org/toolkit). Copyright 2025 by TeachAI. Putting People First AI empowers teachers and students， keeping humans in control. Humans retain ultimate responsibility for all decisions and outcomes. Upholding Learning with Integrity AI is a partner in ethical and transparent learning. Students use AI ethically and transparently to spark ideas and deepen understanding. Cultivating Future-Ready Growth Preparing students for an AI-integrated world. We build AI literacy by teaching students how AI works， how to use it responsibly， and how to evaluate its output to ensure success in college， careers， and life. Safeguarding Safety and Privacy Protecting student data and identity. We strictly select and utilize AI tools that meet rigorous data privacy and digital footprint standards. Advancing Fair and Equal Access Prioritizing fair and equal access to ensure all students have access to AI tools. We provide equitable access to high-quality tools that meet diverse learning needs and help every student reach their full potential. Prioritizing Active Monitoring Regularly reviewing AI use for effectiveness and safety. We evaluate AI tools and monitor school usage to ensure that these technologies always enhance learning， protect users， and uphold high ethical standards. PRIVACY & SECURITY To safeguard student privacy， ensure instructional integrity， and boost professional productivity， please follow these guidelines for district-approved AI tools (accessible via your district login). Do not use non-approved AI resources for any work-related activities. Student Privacy & Data Protection (FERPA Compliance) In accordance with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and PSJA ISD Board Policy FL (LEGAL)， safeguarding student data is a critical legal requirement. STOP: Under no circumstances should staff enter， upload， paste， or describe identifiable student information into public AI tools or prompts. Treat prompts as data leaving district systems. Even partial information combined with context can make a student identifiable. Examples of Strictly Prohibited Information: Basic Identifiers: Student names (first and last)， Student ID numbers， dates of birth， home addresses， or parent/guardian names. Protected Records: Social Security numbers， disciplinary records， health/medical information， or human resources/payroll info. Academic & Support Data: Grades connected to an identifiable student， or Special Education (IEP) and Section 504 details tied to a specific student. Incident Reporting Protocol If you suspect a data exposure， a security breach， or the misuse of an AI tool， you must report it immediately to mitigate data risk. Report to: PSJA ISD IT Helpdesk Submission Channels: Helpdesk Portal Link | helpdesk@psjaisd.us STAFF AI EXPECTATIONS Personal AI Account Policy While PSJA ISD requires district-managed credentials for standard work to ensure legal compliance (CIPA， COPPA， FERPA， PPRA)， it recognizes that staff may use personal premium accounts (e.g.， ChatGPT Plus， Gemini Advanced) for advanced features. When doing so， staff must strictly adhere to data privacy guardrails: never enter student Personally Identifiable Information (PII) or confidential district data into an AI account. Staff Security Protocols To ensure network security and data loss prevention， all staff members must adhere to the following operational guardrails: District-Managed Accounts Only: Always log in using official PSJA ISD Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace credentials. Never use personal emails or accounts for district business. Approved Storage Systems: Store and share district documents only within approved environments (Google Drive， SharePoint， OneDrive， Teams). Follow all existing sharing and permission rules. No Unapproved Add-ons: Do not install AI browser extensions， add-ons， or connectors (for Google Workspace or Office 365) without explicit IT administrative approval. Third-Party App Restriction: Staff are prohibited from authorizing third-party apps or granting AI tools permission to access district accounts and data sets. Managed Endpoints Only: If an authorized AI tool requires file uploads or document access， it must only be accessed on managed district devices equipped with active endpoint protection. Basic Identifiers: Passwords， access tokens， or any login credentials for district-managed systems must never be shared into AI tools. Always follow district guidelines for safe， responsible， and effective use of AI. District Approved AI Tools Information Technology Department maintains a vetted list of AI domains and applications. AI tools and related web traffic will be actively logged and inappropriate content will be blocked on district networks and managed devices. Approved Tools Include: ChatGPT， Microsoft Copilot， Gemini， MagicSchool AI， NotebookLM， Wayground， Khanmigo， Canva AI， Adobe Express， Diffit， Brisk， Curipod， TeachShare. New tools for consideration must be requested and approved by the Information Technology Department (Send Requests to: PSJA ISD IT Helpdesk | helpdesk@psjaisd.us ). Before using any AI tool， confirm: You are using a district-approved AI tool and a district-managed account. No passwords， access tokens， or login credentials are included. No student-identifiable information is included. No confidential staff information is included. Output has been fact-checked. Content aligns with TEKS and district curriculum. You have reviewed and edited the response. Follow all Communications Department Guidelines on use of district branding. STUDENT AI EXPECTATIONS To ensure every PSJA ISD student is prepared to participate， compete， and excel in a global society， the district has established clear guidelines for student engagement with Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). Student AI Commitments LEADER I act honestly and practice good digital citizenship in all my interactions. CHANGE AGENT I learn and adjust to new tools and keep growing in a changing world. VISIONARY IMPLEMENTER I think critically， create original work and innovate with AI. COMMUNITY DEVELOPER I use AI to collaborate respectfully and make a positive impact on my community. PSJA Student AI Quick Guide You are the Pilot. AI is the Co-Pilot. Humans in the Lead. You are responsible for your work and must verify all AI-generated output for accuracy. DO DON'T Ask permission Cite all use Fact-check everything No private info (ID， name， address) No copy & paste No cyberbullying The Privacy Shield: Never enter your Full Name， Student ID， or Home Address into an AI tool. ACADEMIC INTEGRITY Students must always ensure they have explicit permission from their teacher before utilizing Generative AI tools for any coursework. When used， its assistance must be openly disclosed with proper attribution. Activities requiring disclosure or citation include: Quoting， paraphrasing， or summarizing text generated by AI. Incorporating AI-generated images， graphics， video， or audio into projects. Using AI for brainstorming， structuring outlines， conducting preliminary research， or proofreading/editing drafts. HOW TO ATTRIBUTE GEN AI USAGE The type and depth of citation required depend entirely on the assignment and the teacher's expectations: Formal Assignments (Essays， Research Papers): Require a full bibliographic citation (such as MLA or APA) in the Works Cited or References list， alongside in-text citations. Informal Assignments (Presentations， Group Projects， Short Writing): Require a simple disclosure statement detailing how the AI was used. SAMPLE CITATION (MLA FORMAT) Format: Prompt， name of tool， version of tool， company， date of generation， general URL of tool ”Can you explain the difference between mitosis and meiosis using a simple sports analogy? Please don't give me a long essay; just break it down into bullet points.” ChatGPT， 4， June 2026， https://chatgpt.com. SAMPLE DISCLOSURE OF AI USE The sample disclosure might be used at the beginning， or at the end， of an AI-enhanced document: Brainstormed ideas and narrowed down topic using Gemini Asked for an analogy to better understand using ChatGPT Edited and proofread final draft using Gemini CITING TEXT & IMAGES Cite text and images in presentations with a note naming the tool and prompt used， as well as the year. Image generated with Gemini using the prompt ”duck on a pond，” 2026 For more details on MLA citation with AI: https://style.mla.org/citing-generative-ai/ For more information on APA citation with AI: https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/how-to-cite-chatgpt USING AI RESPONSIBLY: EXAMPLES OF MISUSE The following behaviors are considered inappropriate and may result in disciplinary action depending on severity and intent: Academic Dishonesty / Plagiarism: Using AI to generate essays， responses， or projects without teacher permission or failing to cite AI assistance when required. Cheating on Assessments: Using AI tools during quizzes， tests， or exams to obtain answers or complete work dishonestly. Cyberbullying or Harassment: Using AI to generate harmful messages， impersonate individuals， or target students or staff with offensive content. Deepfakes or Manipulated Media: Creating or sharing AI-generated images， videos， or audio intended to mislead， embarrass， or deceive others. Inappropriate or Explicit Content Generation: Using AI tools to produce violent， sexual， or otherwise inappropriate material. Privacy Violations: Entering or sharing personal， confidential， or sensitive information about self or others into AI platforms without authorization. Security Violations / Hacking Attempts: Using AI to attempt unauthorized access to school systems， accounts， or restricted data. Misinformation and Disinformation: Using AI to generate or distribute false or misleading information that could disrupt school operations or harm individuals or the school community. When students are uncertain about appropriate AI use， they are expected to seek guidance from teachers， counselors， or campus administrators. STOP: Misuse of AI tools is considered a violation of the PSJA ISD Student Code of Conduct and will be addressed in alignment with district disciplinary procedures and campus-level implementation guidance. title: Guidelines for AI Integration Throughout Education in the Commonwealth of Virginia (Office of the Secretary of Education)
full_text: GUIDELINES FOR AI INTEGRATION THROUGHOUT EDUCATION IN THE COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA Artificial intelligence (AI) brings tremendous potential to transform education at all levels. By enabling more efficient， universal， and deeper learning， AI can unlock new realms of knowledge that were previously unimaginable. This emerging technology promises to catalyze business innovation and economic growth for the Commonwealth. However， AI also poses risks that must be carefully managed. As we integrate these powerful tools into our schools and workplaces， we must urgently equip students and workers with the skills， knowledge， and competencies to harness AI responsibly and effectively. Our education system must adapt to prepare a workforce that can leverage AI to its full potential while safeguarding against its risks. While AI tools can analyze information and enhance certain aspects of learning with unmatched efficiency， we must remember that education is ultimately a human endeavor. The true art of teaching involves wisdom， judgment and interpersonal skills that machines cannot replicate. As such， AI should never fully replace teachers， who nurture students’ critical thinking， values and character development. Virginia is well-positioned for this new era. The most critical national security and military intelligence institutions in the United States are headquartered in Virginia and the Commonwealth’s colleges and universities lead the nation in technology research and development. These unique factors provide Virginia with a responsibility to spearhead a policy environment that strengthens trust， safety， and security in the development and deployment of AI technologies and the opportunity to assemble experts from the workplace and education to provide ongoing guidance and assistance in the responsible and effective implementation of AI in our education， training， and workplace learning. Guidelines to Support the Responsible & Effective Implementation of AI Across Education in Virginia These Guidelines for AI Integration through Education are comprised of the following three key components: 1) Guiding Principles 2) Strategies for Success 3) Roles and Responsibilities 1. Guiding Principles for the Use of AI in Education • Do no harm: All integration of AI in education must be in accordance with the policy and IT standards that are set forth in the Executive Order and in other state and federal policies. This includes ensuring the safeguarding of the privacy， security， and confidentiality of personally identifiable information， ensuring that algorithms are not based on inherent biases that lead to discriminatory outcomes， and that AI is only allowed when its use has the potential to contribute positive good/improvement to the status quo. • Prioritize integrity: A core purpose of education is the development of responsible， ethical， and engaged citizens. Therefore， part of the integration of AI in education must be to teach about morality， ethics， honor， cheating， and how artificial intelligence can lead to perverse and destructive outcomes for individuals， relationships， and communities. • Augment， not replace humans: AI cannot and should not ever replace human judgement. Although synthesis and analysis of information can be expedited through AI， it will never replace teachers who provide wisdom， context， feedback， empathy， nurturing and humanity in ways that a machine cannot. It also should not overpower/over-ride the critical thinking， judgement， and morality of the learner. • Harness AI to empower student success: AI presents transformative opportunities to enrich instruction and enable more adaptive， personalized learning. To fully leverage these benefits， we must embrace an outlook of innovation and experimentation， while ensuring access for all learners. Rather than just digitizing traditional practices， we can reimagine education to nurture each student’s unlimited potential with the assistive power of AI. Our vision should focus on possibility - AI as a gateway to expand human capacity - not conformity to conventions of the past. • Work in partnership: AI researchers and experts in Virginia colleges and universities and employers are key partners and guides around building the skills and knowledge required to be successful in the new economy. This includes how to think about evolving AI systems and the practices needed to use them responsibly. • Be constantly discerning and responsive to the continuous expansion of AI capabilities and uses: This is not a one-and-done. The guidelines， best practices， and tools available will constantly need to be revisited to keep pace with the changes brought by the exponential growth of AI and technology advancements in our world. Nimbleness and urgency， balanced with careful considerations， will be critical to ensuring we are as prepared for the continuous change ahead in education. 2. Strategies for Successful Integration of AI in Education At every level of education—from governing boards to individual classrooms—these strategies can improve the effective integration of AI into education. Encourage Exploration — To have informed discussions about integrating AI， educators first need hands- on experience to understand these technologies’ capabilities and limitations. School leaders should actively facilitate opportunities for teacher teams to directly explore various AI tools. Through guided firsthand usage， educators can discover potential applications to enrich instruction， as well as critical risks and challenges to consider. Rather than rely on rumors or superficial perceptions， we must empower teachers with deeper practical knowledge. By allocating time and resources for structured experimentation， schools can tap into educators’ insights to uncover creative use cases while proactively addressing ethical concerns. This ground-up understanding， straight from classroom trenches， will produce more thoughtful and responsible approaches to adopting AI. 1. Provide Professional Development — As with any new tool or strategy， educators need professional development from experts in order to feel comfortable using it. Offering workshops or professional development courses， micro-credentials， or micro-badges on AI as well as meaningful follow-up implementation and application activities ，discussions and opportunities to collaborate with colleagues and experts who can help teachers understand and experience its capabilities and limitations. can help teachers understand and experience its capabilities and limitations. 2. Spotlight Success — Spotlight interesting examples of AI that are already being used in schools. Ensure educators have meaningful outlets to share what they are trying and whether it is working or not. Encourage teachers to collaborate in their exploration of AI to learn from each other's experiences and builds a supportive community for this new educational environment. 3. Host Stakeholder Conversations — Host regular conversations with business leaders， educators， governing members， leaders， and families about AI and how schools are preparing or will be preparing students with the skills to thrive in an AI-infused world. Topics could include， but not limited to， fostering ethical AI use and digital citizenship collaboration and interdisciplinary learning， and integration of AI in the curriculum. 4. Set The Right Conditions — When it comes to using AI or any other technologies in school， it is important to establish conditions for effective use. Clearly outline the school or system’s policies and protocols around data privacy， honor code， student code of conduct， acceptable use， and ethical considerations when using AI， including those related to plagiarism and proper use of secondary sources. Teachers should know what is expected of them and the boundaries within which they should operate. These conditions might include using technology to support teaching and learning.1 3. Roles & Responsibilities Education stakeholders must understand and embrace their roles and responsibilities in an effort to integrate AI into our education institutions. This is an initial list of those roles and responsibilities which will continue to be refined by the Advisory Group. ▪ State Education Agencies – Virginia Department of Education (VDOE) and State Council of Higher Education for Virginia (SCHEV) (including Virginia Community College System) ▪ Governing Boards/Leadership – 131 K-12 school division boards of education and division leaderships and the boards of visitors/presidents/leadership teams at every public college and university ▪ Higher Education Programs and Faculty/School & Classroom Leaders ▪ AI/Technology Directors Specific Roles of State Agencies: VDOE and SCHEV shall meet monthly with the SOE team to identify implementation hurdles， best practices， and areas of support needed from the field by the agencies to support implementation， accelerate what’s working well， and improve oversight of AI in education in the Commonwealth. A. Each agency shall on an ongoing basis: 1 This list is adapted from the following report: https://www.naesp.org/resource/5-strategies-for-success-in- bringing-ai-to-schools/ a. Create advisory resources， including policy and protocols best practices， for generative AI2 that are continuously updated and modified. b. Create processes for tiers and rules at which approval is given for use of AI tools. c. Develop stakeholder training toolkits and workshops for governing bodies， educators， families， and students on AI， its capabilities， and its limitations. d. Spotlight success stories where AI is being used well in schools or higher education institutions. Serve as a resource bank of what is working and provide a supportive learning community for interested educators or leaders. e. Host conversations with educators， institution leaders， and governing board members on how schools can best prepare students with the skills to thrive in an AI-infused world on topics such as fostering ethical AI use and digital citizenship; integration of AI in the curriculum; or establishing policy conditions for effective use. f. Modify agency staffing structure to better provide expertise to the field， including on what AI tools are most applicable and encouraged to be used for K-12 or higher education institutions. B. These agencies in partnership with the Virginia Community College System shall work in collaboration to design micro-badging and micro-credential training opportunities for the field to stay abreast of the latest AI technologies， ethics， and best governance leadership skills. C. Ongoing Roles and Responsibilities: a. Capacity building/training at every agency and throughout the sector to the classroom level. b. Safeguarding privacy， security， and confidentiality of data. c. Strengthening governance of AI through supporting capacity building and technical assistance to the boards of visitors or school division governing boards. Specific roles of Governing Boards/Leadership and Educators: Education happens at the local level. The role of informed and engaged governing bodies， active leaders and informed and empowered faculty and staff at the institution or school/division level will determine how well AI is integrated and sued in education in Virginia. The following roles and responsibilities will help ensure the local implementation is constantly monitored， actively managed， and continuously adjusted to address the ongoing changes AI will bring to education. These are the critical but not comprehensive roles and responsibilities at the point of education delivery: 1. Establish a culture of integrity o Define what this culture looks like (State Agencies and Governing Boards) o Build a culture of integrity by discussing the honor code often with students and parents， implementing an honor code system with real consequences (Faculty/Staff) 2. Follow an Acceptable Use Policy inside and outside the classroom o Codify Acceptable Use Policy (State Agencies/Governing Boards) o Review and discuss the Acceptable Use Policy with students and parents (Faculty/Staff) o Implement and hold learning community accountable for living up to Acceptable Use Policy (Faculty/Staff) 3. Design assignments and assessments that encourage critical thinking and original thought and human judgement (Faculty/Staff) 2 Similar to Oregon’s Developing Policy and Protocols for the use of Generative AI in K-12 Classrooms resource or Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in K-12 Classrooms resource for K-12 and Higher Education. 4. Create opportunities for collaboration and peer review (Faculty/Staff) 5. Integrate digital citizenship with the following Standards of Learning strands (VDOE， Governing Boards， and Faculty/Staff) o Computer Science: The Impacts of Computing o Digital Learning Integration: Digital Citizen o English: Communication and Multimodal Literacies， Research o Fine Arts: Innovation in the Arts， History， Culture， and Citizenship o Health: Safety/Injury Prevention o Mathematics: Computation o Science: Scientific and Engineering Practices: Obtaining， evaluating， and communicating information o Social Studies and History: Skills o World Language: Interacting in School and Global Communities 6. Clarify expectations for use of AI in assignments (Governing Boards) 7. Communicate clearly and specifically when and how students can utilize Generative Artificial Intelligence in assignments (Faculty/Staff)

title: Artificial Intelligence Guidance for FCPS Faculty and Staff (Fairfax County Public Schools)
full_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how we work， teach， learn， and communicate. In Fairfax County Public Schools (FCPS)， we use AI thoughtfully， responsibly， and in support of our mission to prepare students for success in a changing world. This handbook is designed to help staff understand when and how AI can be used， what expectations apply， and where to find practical support. It is not meant to replace professional judgment. Instead， it provides guidance， examples， and resources that help staff make informed decisions aligned with FCPS values， policies， and priorities. Our Approach to AI in FCPS Fairfax County Public Schools (FCPS) is committed to using artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance teaching， learning， and operations in ways that are ethical， responsible， and student-centered. Our approach is guided by human expertise， responsible innovation， and a commitment to developing AI literacy for all. As a community of educators and learners， we share responsibility for using AI thoughtfully and purposefully to maximize benefits， reduce risks， and prepare students for a future where AI is increasingly part of everyday life. The following principles guide every decision we make about AI in FCPS. Open all Keep Humans in Control of Decisions AI may support decisions， but it does not replace educator expertise， school leadership， or professional responsibility. Develop AI literacy， knowledge， and skills to use AI as a tool to support education and operations. Recognize humans as experts who are responsible for learning and decision-making. Be responsive to user needs and questions about the use of AI. Leverage AI Tools Ethically and Responsibly AI should be used in ways that protect privacy， support learning， uphold academic integrity， and avoid harm. Improve learning， develop Portrait of a Graduate skills， and uphold academic integrity. Promote wellness and safety， environmental stewardship， transparency， inclusivity， and equity . Respect human rights， recognize and address bias， and broaden perspectives. Protect privacy ， security ， and data rights of people in our community. Intentionally Enhance Our Use of Emerging Technology When used well， emerging technology can reduce routine tasks， support differentiation， improve access， and help staff focus more time on the work that matters most. Select technology tools， including AI， that support responsible use and prepare students for the future. Regularly check， question， and evaluate the use of emerging technologies， such as AI， and what they produce. Continuously monitor the impacts of emerging technologies like AI to maximize benefits， avoid harm， and spark innovation. Every FCPS employee plays a role in ensuring AI is used safely， ethically， and effectively. Whether supporting instruction， communicating with families， planning lessons， or completing operational tasks， staff are responsible for using AI in ways that reflect FCPS values， policies， and professional standards. The expectations below apply to all staff members and should guide every use of AI. Open all Protect Data and Privacy Protecting students， staff， and confidential information is a shared responsibility. Staff are expected to: Never enter personally identifiable， confidential， or sensitive information into unapproved AI tools. Use only approved AI tools when working with protected information. Follow all applicable FCPS policies， state and federal laws， and data privacy requirements. Report suspected privacy or security concerns through established FCPS procedures. What This Looks Like In Practice Appropriate Use Drafting a family newsletter without student information. Creating lesson ideas using general prompts. Brainstorming instructional strategies. Not Appropriate Uploading student work containing names to an unapproved AI tool. Entering IEP， 504， disciplinary， or personnel information into public AI tools. Use AI Responsibly AI supports professional work; it does not replace professional judgment. Staff are expected to: Keep humans in control of instructional and operational decisions. Review AI-generated content for accuracy， bias， accessibility， and appropriateness. Apply professional judgment before sharing or using AI-generated materials. Respect copyright， intellectual property， and the work of others. Use AI ethically and transparently. What This Looks Like In Practice Use AI to: brainstorm draft organize summarize differentiate generate ideas Do not use AI to: make professional decisions for you make grading determinations replace your expertise produce final work without careful review Check AI Tool Approval Before Use Not all AI tools have been reviewed for FCPS use. Staff are expected to: Verify approval in the Digital Ecosystem Library (DEL) . Note: Log in to view staff-only tools. Follow the approved audience and usage guidance. Use only approved AI tools on FCPS devices and networks. If a tool is not approved， do not use it for FCPS work involving students or confidential information. Set Clear Student AI Use Expectations FCPS recognizes that students may have access to AI tools on personal devices. Staff need to indicate if students are able to optionally use AI on an assignment. If a student chooses to use AI on a personal device outside of school for school-related work， students are expected to follow their teacher's directions， the school’s Honor Code， the Student Rights and Responsibilities (SR&R) ， and all applicable FCPS policies. It is also important to get parent or guardian permission. Staff are expected to communicate clearly: when AI is permitted when AI is prohibited how AI should be acknowledged how students should demonstrate their own thinking expectations for responsible AI use Promote Ethical AI Use and Academic Integrity AI should support learning， not replace it. Staff are expected to: Design learning experiences that prioritize student thinking. Encourage critical thinking and creativity. Ensure assessments provide evidence of student understanding. Address inappropriate AI use as a learning opportunity whenever appropriate. AI use is not automatically an Honor Code violation. Consider the purpose of the assignment， the expectations communicated to students， and the evidence of authentic learning. Model Responsible AI Use Students learn from the examples adults set. Staff are expected to: Demonstrate thoughtful and ethical AI use. Explain how AI supports professional work when appropriate. Discuss the strengths and limitations of AI. Encourage curiosity， questioning， and responsible decision-making. Model digital citizenship and AI literacy in everyday practice. Reinforce with students that AI should not replace trusted relationships or support from caring adults， and should not be used for mental health care， counseling， or help during a crisis or safety concern. Artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance professional practice by supporting planning， instruction， communication， collaboration， and productivity. When used thoughtfully， AI can reduce time spent on routine tasks， allowing staff to focus on the work that matters most， building relationships， supporting students， and creating meaningful learning experiences. The examples below illustrate ways approved AI tools can support common professional workflows. They are intended as starting points. Staff remain responsible for selecting appropriate tools， protecting privacy， reviewing AI-generated content， and applying professional judgment. Open all Planning AI can help you: Brainstorm ideas Develop lesson or meeting plans Organize projects Create agendas Build timelines FCPS Prompt Starter Help me develop a lesson plan for [grade] [subject] on [topic]. Include a lesson hook， learning objective， formative assessment， and one differentiation strategy aligned to the Virginia Standards of Learning. Teaching and Learning AI can help you: Differentiate instruction Generate discussion questions Create exemplars Support Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Suggest enrichment and intervention ideas FCPS Prompt Starter Suggest three ways to teach [concept] using different instructional approaches. Include one scaffold for multilingual learners and one accommodation for students who need additional support. Assessment and Feedback AI can help you: Draft rubrics Generate exit tickets Create reflection prompts Develop success criteria FCPS Prompt Starter Create five exit ticket questions that measure student understanding of [learning objective] at varying levels of cognitive demand. Communication AI can help you: Draft newsletters Prepare emails Summarize meetings Develop presentations Translate general communications using approved tools FCPS Prompt Starter Draft a family newsletter explaining this week's learning in clear， family-friendly language. Keep the tone positive， concise， and welcoming. Collaboration and Leadership AI can help you: Plan professional learning Develop meeting agendas Organize coaching conversations Brainstorm solutions Summarize information FCPS Prompt Starter Create a meeting agenda for a collaborative team focused on [goal]. Include discussion questions， action items， and opportunities for reflection. Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how students access information， generate ideas， and demonstrate learning. While AI presents new opportunities and challenges， the foundations of effective instruction remain the same. In FCPS， AI should strengthen， not replace， the instructional practices that develop student thinking， creativity， collaboration， and authentic learning. The FCPS Learning Model and Portrait of a Graduate continue to guide instructional decision-making， with AI serving as one tool that can support these priorities. This section describes how educators can thoughtfully integrate AI into instruction while keeping learning， human judgment， and student growth at the center. Open all Instructional Shifts for the AI Era The availability of AI changes how students complete tasks， but it does not change the purpose of teaching. Effective instruction increasingly emphasizes the thinking that students must do themselves. Examles of Instructional Shifts Instructional Shift What It Looks Like Promote Classroom Discourse Students discuss， debate， question， and build understanding together. Ask for Justification， Not Just Answers Students explain reasoning， defend decisions， and critique AI-generated responses. Embed Thinking Routines Students make their thinking visible through questioning， reflection， and evidence-based reasoning. Center Collaboration Students solve problems together and learn from multiple perspectives. Value Process as Much as Product Students document their thinking through drafts， revisions， reflections， and responsible AI use. Advancing the FCPS Learning Model The FCPS Learning Model remains the foundation for high-quality instruction. AI can help educators strengthen each component while maintaining a focus on authentic student learning. How AI Can Support Staff By Learning Model Domain Domain AI Can Support Educators By Universally Designed Curriculum Generating multiple representations， scaffolds， translations， visuals， and accessible supports. Meaningful Learning Experiences Creating dilemmas， inquiry experiences， real-world connections， and authentic problem-solving opportunities. Learner-Centered Environment Supporting differentiation， collaboration， discussion， and multiple pathways to learning. Purposeful Assessment Making student thinking visible through reflection， revision， annotation， and authentic demonstrations of learning. Educator AI Literacies Effective instruction begins with informed educators. Educator AI Literacies provide a shared framework that helps educators make human-centered instructional decisions while supporting student AI literacy. Educator AI Literacy Domains The Educator AI Literacies are organized using Digital Promise’s three Modes of Engagement ， and put into three domains: Understand AI Develop an accurate understanding of what AI is， how it works， and its capabilities and limitations. Evaluate AI Apply professional judgment by verifying AI outputs， protecting privacy， and considering ethics， bias， and transparency. Use AI Integrate AI intentionally to support learning while preserving student thinking， ownership， and meaningful engagement. Technology continues to transform how students learn， communicate， create， and participate in the world. As access to artificial intelligence (AI) continues to expand， students need more than technical skills. They need the knowledge， skills， and mindsets to use technology thoughtfully， responsibly， and effectively. FCPS recognizes that AI literacy is one part of a broader vision for digital literacy. Rather than treating AI as a separate initiative， FCPS prepares students to understand and use AI as one component of becoming digitally literate citizens， learners， creators， and problem-solvers. Open all What is Digital Literacy? FCPS defines digital literacy as: The knowledge， skills， and mindsets to use technology safely， responsibly， and effectively in order to learn， create， connect， and participate in a digital world. Digital literacy prepares students to think critically， evaluate information， communicate responsibly， and make informed decisions in an increasingly digital society. Why Digital Literacy Matters FCPS believes students must develop digital literacy while remaining grounded in the human skills that technology cannot replace. Our approach is rooted in the FCPS Strategic Plan by supporting: Goal 1: Foundational academic skills， curiosity， and joy for learning. Goal 2: Students who are safe， supported， included， and empowered. Goal 3: Academic growth and excellence. Goal 4: Equitable access and opportunity. Goal 5: Innovation that prepares students for the future. Digital literacy helps students become thoughtful learners， responsible digital citizens， and adaptable problem-solvers in a rapidly changing world. FCPS Commitment As we implement the FCPS Digital Literacy Curriculum， we are committed to: Keeping people at the center of teaching， learning， and decision-making. Leveraging technology tools ethically and responsibly. Intentionally evaluating emerging technologies before use with students. Balancing technology-enhanced learning with meaningful non-digital experiences that support relationships， inquiry， creativity， and well-being. These commitments align with the FCPS AI Principles (above) and guide how AI is integrated into teaching and learning. The FCPS Digital Literacy Curriculum The FCPS Digital Literacy Curriculum builds early awareness， shared language， and responsible decision-making that develops over time. Students build safe， thoughtful， and responsible habits before they are expected to use increasingly sophisticated digital tools independently. The curriculum is organized around four areas of learning. Digital Citizenship Students develop the knowledge and skills to make intentional， responsible， safe， and ethical choices in digital environments. Information Literacy Students develop the knowledge and skills to identify information needs and to locate， critically evaluate， and use information from a variety of sources. Media Literacy Students develop the critical thinking skills to analyze， evaluate， and communicate media messages in safe， ethical， and socially responsible ways. AI Literacy Students develop the knowledge and skills to understand how AI， technology， and digital systems shape their lives， learning， and society. AI literacy is taught through both dedicated lessons and integrated learning experiences. How the Curriculum Is Implemented Digital literacy is intentionally embedded throughout the K to 12 experience using developmentally appropriate instruction. Grades K to 6: Digital literacy lessons are delivered through specials and/or classroom-facilitated learning experiences. Grades 7 to 12: Digital literacy concepts are integrated into English Language Arts instruction and reinforced through supplemental lessons in Advisory. This approach ensures students develop a common foundation while applying digital literacy skills in authentic learning experiences across grade levels and content areas. AI Literacy Within Digital Literacy AI literacy builds on the knowledge and skills students develop through digital citizenship， information literacy， and media literacy. Students learn to: understand how AI works and recognize its capabilities and limitations evaluate AI-generated information critically identify bias， inaccuracies， and missing perspectives make informed decisions about when and how AI should be used use AI thoughtfully， responsibly， and effectively These concepts are introduced through dedicated AI literacy lessons and reinforced through integrated learning experiences across the curriculum. The Role of Educators Every educator contributes to students' digital literacy development. Educators support digital literacy by: Modeling responsible technology and AI use. Integrating digital literacy into authentic learning experiences. Helping students think critically about digital information and AI-generated content. Creating opportunities for students to communicate， collaborate， create， and solve problems responsibly. Reinforcing ethical， safe， and effective technology use across learning environments. Helping students understand AI's limitations， including that AI does not have genuine understanding or empathy and should not be used for mental health care， counseling， or help during a crisis or safety concern. Whether teaching a dedicated digital literacy lesson or integrating concepts into everyday instruction， educators play an essential role in preparing students for a digital world. Looking Ahead Digital literacy is essential to preparing students for learning， work， and civic life. As technology continues to evolve， FCPS will continue to equip students with the knowledge， skills， and mindsets needed to navigate digital environments with confidence， responsibility， and purpose. AI literacy is an important part of that preparation， but it is most effective when taught as part of a comprehensive approach to digital literacy that values human thinking， meaningful relationships， ethical decision-making， and lifelong learning. Academic integrity is built on honesty， responsibility， and authentic learning. Artificial intelligence (AI) presents new opportunities and challenges， but it does not change the purpose of learning or assessment: providing meaningful evidence of what students know， understand， and can do. Educators play an important role in establishing clear expectations， promoting integrity， and helping students understand their responsibilities when AI becomes part of their learning. Open all Current FCPS Guidance for Student AI Use Students may not use unapproved AI tools on FCPS-issued devices. FCPS recognizes that students may have access to AI tools on personal devices. This handbook does not encourage or authorize the use of those tools. It provides guidance to help educators support students and respond consistently if AI becomes part of student work. If a student chooses to use AI on a personal device outside of school for school-related work， students are expected to: Follow their teacher's directions. Follow the school's Honor Code. Follow the Student Rights and Responsibilities (SR&R) . Follow all applicable FCPS policies. Obtain parent or guardian permission. Building a Culture of Integrity Academic integrity is most effectively supported through a classroom culture that values learning， reflection， and responsible decision-making. Focus on Learning Frame assignments around meaningful learning goals that emphasize critical thinking， creativity， communication， and problem-solving. Reinforce that the purpose of every assignment is to develop student understanding， not simply complete a task. Model Responsible AI Use Model thoughtful and ethical AI use in your own professional practice. When appropriate， demonstrate how to question AI outputs， verify information， recognize bias， and improve AI-generated ideas through human thinking and professional judgment. Promote a Growth Mindset Conversations about AI should be opportunities for learning and reflection. When concerns arise， help students understand expectations and strengthen responsible decision-making rather than focusing solely on rule enforcement. Setting Clear Expectations Teacher expectations come first. Recognizing that students may have access to AI tools outside of school， it is important to communicate clearly whether AI is permitted for a specific assignment and， if so， how it may be used. Clearly communicate: whether AI is permitted for the assignment when AI is not permitted how students should demonstrate their own thinking how students should explain or cite AI use as required when use is permitted AI expectations may differ from one assignment to another. If AI is permitted， students remain responsible for following the assignment expectations and demonstrating their own learning. If a student chooses to use AI on a personal device outside of school for school-related work， students are expected to follow their teacher's directions， the school’s Honor Code， the Student Rights and Responsibilities (SR&R)， and all applicable FCPS policies. It is also important for students to discuss with their parents/caregiver before they use an AI tool. Sample Syllabus Language Option if AI will not be allowed AI should not be used on any assignment completed for this class. Option if AI Will be Allowed Under Certain Conditions FCPS recognizes that students may have access to AI tools on personal devices outside of school. In this class， the teacher will communicate to students if optional use of AI is allowed and， if so， how AI can be used. If a teacher does not indicate AI use is permitted， students should assume that it is not. If a student chooses to use AI on a personal device outside of school for school-related work， students are expected to follow their teacher's directions， the school’s Honor Code， the Student Rights and Responsibilities (SR&R) ， and all applicable FCPS policies. It is also important for students to discuss with parents or guardians before using an AI tool. Supporting Student Reflection When AI has been used appropriately， reflection helps students think about how AI influenced their learning while reinforcing transparency and metacognition. When appropriate， ask students to explain: What did you do before using AI? How did you use AI? What decisions did you make after using AI? How did AI support your learning? Reflection should demonstrate that the student remained the decision-maker throughout the learning process. Sample Student Reflection Statements I used AI to brainstorm three ideas， but I chose [insert the idea chosen] because it connected to my own experience. I asked AI to summarize a passage， then rewrote it in my own words to check my understanding. AI generated practice questions， but I solved them on my own before reviewing the answers. I asked AI to summarize a passage in two different ways. I noticed both summaries included X， Y， and Z. I then wrote my own summary that also included those features. Resource: FCPS Student Guide to AI Responding When Concerns Arise When student work raises questions， begin with curiosity， not accusation. Invite students to explain their thinking， describe their process， share drafts， or discuss how they approached the assignment. These conversations often reveal opportunities to reteach responsible AI use， citation practices， revision strategies， or expectations for academic integrity. Possible Indicators of AI Use These are clues， not proof. A student cannot explain or demonstrate their thinking. Writing differs significantly from the student's typical voice or level of detail. Drafts show little evidence of revision or sudden jumps in quality. Sources cannot be verified or appear fabricated. Avoid AI Detection Tools AI detection tools are unreliable， may create privacy concerns， and are not endorsed by FCPS. Professional judgment and authentic conversations remain the most effective way to address concerns. If academic dishonesty is confirmed， partner with school administration and follow the school’s Honor Code and Student Rights and Responsibilities (SR&R). When appropriate， prioritize reteaching and provide students opportunities to demonstrate their learning. Partnering with Families Families play an important role in supporting responsible technology use and academic integrity. Share classroom expectations with families and encourage conversations about responsible technology use， learning， and student ownership. Resources FCPS Student Guide to AI Partnering with Families Resources (below) Student Rights and Responsibilities (SR&R) Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) This section helps educators provide families with clear， supportive， and consistent messages about AI use in FCPS. The goal is to build trust， emphasize shared responsibility， and empower families to make informed choices. Open all Key Messages for Families FCPS recognizes that students have access to AI tools on personal devices and may choose to use them for school-related work outside of school. This guide explains the expectations students must follow if they choose to use AI. AI supports learning， not replaces it. Students remain responsible for their ideas and understanding， and the school’s Honor Code and SR&R always apply. AI use is not required. Teachers will clarify when AI can be used and how students should document or explain their use. Protecting student data and privacy is a shared priority between schools and families. Ready-to-Use Communication Messages you can copy， adapt， and send. Sample Teacher Message to Caregivers For the start of the year or when introducing AI in class. Dear Families， FCPS recognizes that students may have access to AI tools on personal devices and may want to use them on their assignments. If optional use of AI is allowed， I will explain how it can be used and how students should show their process. The focus will always be on your child’s ideas and understanding. Students should also talk to their parents or caregiver before using AI as well. Students remain responsible for their own work， and our Honor Code and SR&R apply. Thank you for partnering with us as we help students learn how to use AI responsibly. Making Informed Choices About AI Tools Dear Families， FCPS recognizes that students may have access to AI tools on personal devices and may want to use it when completing assignments at home. While teachers will not require students to use AI tools， some students may decide to use AI tools on their own. We encourage families to talk to their children about using AI safely， responsibly， and appropriately. Ask these quick questions together: What happens to the data? Does the tool collect， share， or store personal information? Who owns the work? Will your child keep rights to their writing， images， or projects once entered? Can data be deleted later? Is there an option to remove information if you change your mind? Is it age-appropriate? Many tools have age requirements (often 13+ or 18+). Reviewing privacy policies and terms of service helps your child build responsible digital habits and keeps their ideas at the center of learning. Thank you for partnering with us in guiding students to use AI responsibly. For Newsletters or Schoology Use this when you need a concise update: FCPS recognizes that students may have access to AI tools on personal devices. In FCPS， AI supports learning but never replaces student work. Teachers will clarify when AI can be used， and students remain responsible for their original ideas and understanding. Ideas for Family Conversations When speaking with families (e.g.， at Back-to-School Night， parent conferences， or casual conversations)， these points can keep the message consistent and clear: AI can support learning but is not a shortcut. Students may be asked to include an “Explanation of AI Use.” Most AI tools are designed for ages 13+ (some 18+). Families decide what’s appropriate at home. Teachers will only use AI tools approved in the DEL . No student will be required to use unapproved tools. Guidance on Personal Devices Students may access AI tools on personal devices outside of school. Families play an important role in guiding safe and responsible use. How Families Can Support Read the tool’s terms of service and privacy policy with your child. Discuss what kind of information the tool collects， how it may be used， and whether data can be deleted. Confirm age requirements for use. Talk about who owns the work once it’s entered and whether rights remain with the student. Encourage your child to pause and ask: “What information am I sharing， and do I feel comfortable with this?” Building Digital Citizenship Together Explore tools as a family to highlight both their strengths and limitations. Use reviews of privacy policies as opportunities to practice digital literacy skills. Support thoughtful use so students retain ownership of their work and ideas.
