EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 6 Understanding Artificial Intelligence The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education starts with the fundamental understanding that AI is not a replacement for human intelligence or humanitarian presence in education. According to UNESCO， AI in education is expected to be a $6 billion worldwide industry in 20241 with estimates of growth reaching $19.9 billion by 20282. LinkedIn’s Economic Graph Research Institute estimates that， by 2030， the skill sets needed for jobs will change by 65%， affecting not just tech， but all industries3. Corporate entities are moving fast to meet the need and demand for products that streamline the delivery of education， but not all products are the same. It is the responsibility of the education community to carefully and strategically understand how these products work， what data is collected， and where information is sourced. While AI is an emerging innovation in education， Local Education Agencies (LEAs) can utilize and build on existing policies that are based on educational integrity， student safety， and proven instructional practices. In conversation， AI tools are often discussed as a holistic， outside influence on education， yet policy regarding AI should not be separately written. Key facets of these tools already apply to concerns such as student data privacy， plagiarism， cyberbullying， and digital literacy， and can be called out within existing and corresponding policies. Whether updating policies， adopting software， delivering instruction， or analyzing outputs， the vital role each of us plays in understanding what AI is and is not cannot be overemphasized. The first step in AI integration is realizing the opportunity for AI to transform the way we access and use information as we learn and work in our world today， as well as into the future. The next step is to ensure all guidance， policies， systems， and instructional practices are grounded on ethical， equitable， and inclusive uses of AI throughout our Washington communities. LEAs must ensure educational and technology standards are applied to meet the needs of all students so that AI tools enhance education. Finally， state and local policymakers and education leaders must act to build an ethical framework of funding to support policies around every student that embraces each student’s unique abilities and allows them to use existing and emerging AI tools in a safe learning environment. 1 United Nations Educational， Scientific and Cultural Organization. Implementing AI in Student Learning When integrating AI into student learning， it’s important to empower students in how and to what degree AI is utilized in their learning journey. By doing so， students can actively participate in shaping their educational experience with AI. • Co-create and share an AI decision-making rubric with students (example rubric). • Support students in taking a human-centered approach to using AI. • Empower students in leveraging AI in scaffolding understanding， feedback， and reflection. • Support students in critically thinking about the role of AI within their learning journey and within their preparation for college， career， and life. • Empower students receiving special education services to use AI to personalize and increase their access to learning. • Integrate ethics and critical thinking activities that align with grade-level and subject-level instruction. • Use AI for differentiation and assessment， including intelligent tutoring systems that allow text to speech， translation， personalized learning， and inquiry-based learning. • Prepare students for jobs of the future， including those in career and technical education (CTE) programs， by partnering with industry to update and integrate learning standards. GUIDANCE 12 Sensitive and Confidential Data Ensure that your LEA AI use complies with student/personal privacy and data protection laws. Be aware of and follow any age restrictions for the use of all AI tools and resources. • Before sharing private data， ensure that the AI tool meets the following requirements: ◦ Family Education Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) requires that schools not disclose personal identifying information of a minor or eligible student without express written consent of the parent or eligible student. ◦ Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) requires schools to obtain parental consent before allowing students under 13 to use online services that collect， use， or disclose personal information. ◦ Children’s Internet Protection Act (CIPA) requires that schools implement an internet safety policy that includes protective measures to block or filter access to obscene or harmful content. • Have a clear understanding of your data collection processes. Update policies to include the use of and considerations for using AI. • Give users options to opt-out or delete their data if they want. GUIDANCE 13 Policy AI policies must promote equitable and inclusive access to AI. Education policymakers must focus on ensuring the use of AI increases the public good， with emphasis on empowering students who are members of communities that have been historically underserved. It is important that policies， by design， enhance a human-centered approach to pedagogy and learning， and respects ethical norms and standards. AI policy and use should be geared to improving learning for every student， empowering teachers， and strengthening learning management systems. Building Human-Centered AI Policies Incorporate the need for human intelligence and responsibility into AI usage policies. All AI use should start， and end， with human insight. • Responsible Use Policy: Known as an acceptable use policy (AUP) or technology use policy， this describes what any person authorized to utilize the district’s technology system may do and not do. It describes the terms and conditions for educational institutions and should be updated to include the safe and appropriate use of AI tools. (A separate AI AUP is not needed.) • AI Inquiry and Input Review: Require human input of data with clear mandates that staff and students should never input personal， sensitive， or confidential data， including any data related to student education records， into any AI system without first ensuring that the system meets FERPA， COPPA， and CIPA requirements. Emphasize the need for review prior to finalizing any information into a system that learns from data entered. • Embrace the Use of Data and the Evaluation of AI Output: Invest in systems that create streamlined opportunities for staff and students to enter information efficiently and safely， allow them to improve instruction， and draw connections to better understand student thinking and learning. • AI Output Review: AI users should review and critically assess outputs from AI tools before sharing or publicizing results， including in the classroom. Staff and students should not rely exclusively on AI-generated content without fact-checking and evaluating results. Ultimately， it is up to human users to determine how AI information is shared and used. ◦ Bias and Misinformation: AI-generated content is based on datasets or data models that may contain biases， false information， or other inaccuracies. AI systems do not have the ability to think or verify accuracy. Therefore， verifying AI results to ensure the source is credible must occur before considering an AI output in academic work. ◦ Safety and Respect: Users must never use AI tools to create misleading or inappropriate content， take someone’s likeness without permission， or harm humans or the community at large. (Note: This may also be added to a student code of conduct or bullying/cyberbullying/harassment policy.) GUIDANCE FOR INTEGRATING AI IN EDUCATION: A HUMAN-CENTERED APPROACH 19 AI Considerations Across K–12 Teaching AI across the K–12 spectrum is crucial for preparing students for a future where AI literacy is a fundamental skill. As children grow， their encounters with AI in daily life and the classroom will shape their understanding of technology and its implications. Introducing AI at an age-appropriate pace ensures students develop critical thinking skills alongside their technical abilities. Educators are key in guiding students through the ethical， practical， and innovative uses of AI， ensuring that as they mature， they are not only proficient in using AI but also in understanding its impact on society and individual identity. Elementary School Students “Artificial Intelligence” importantly includes the term “artificial.” Understanding AI is predicated on understanding that AI is not sentient， but that can be difficult for young kids to discern as virtual assistants like Amazon Alexa and Apple’s Siri are designed to engage with users in a human-like fashion. Furthermore， many children under the age of 13 have access to these technologies and social media platforms – even though there may be usage policies in place prohibiting children from using these tools. Because young children using these tools may be exposed to the same risks as teenagers and adolescents， educators should also be aware of the considerations listed below for middle and high school students. Elementary educators have tools available to mitigate the risks associated with young children using tools that come with AI features. Interactive tools like Google’s Quick， Draw! or Instrument Playground can be fun ways to engage with AI-based technology and bridge foundational understanding about how the tools work. When educators guide students in asking questions of and submitting prompts to large language models， students can receive answers while avoiding potentially inappropriate content. Categorizing the tools kids are already familiar with as AI can be a great starting point to build toward deeper conversations down the road. Middle and High School Students Middle school is a time of significant development for students. As learners， middle school students develop curiosity and critical thinking skills while engaging with challenging subjects. AI tools can complement this developmental stage by engaging students in critically thinking about content and how they can leverage AI tools within their own personal learning journey. Students can analyze output generated by a large language model to discern what flaws the model or even the model’s argument may have. As students progress through high school， they may pursue more advanced studies about how AI is incorporated into society， industry， and policy. Knowledge of AI is increasingly becoming a sought-after skill in workplaces across a variety of fields. Digital literacy， including deeper understanding of the technical and ethical aspects of AI， is an important skill for all students to learn as they consider their post-secondary pathways. AI CONSIDERATIONS ACROSS K–12 20 Framework for Student Critical Thinking about AI Utilizing the SHIFT framework with middle and high school students offers a structured approach to developing critical thinking skills， particularly in the context of leveraging AI tools in their work. By starting with curiosity， students are encouraged to explore AI’s potential and limitations， fostering a questioning attitude toward technology. Honing in on specific details allows them to understand the intricacies and implications of AI applications， encouraging deeper learning. Identifying the context helps students recognize the relevance and impact of AI in various situations， promoting awareness of its societal and ethical dimensions. Framing issues from new perspectives encourages creativity and problem-solving skills， while discussing what’s missing challenges students to identify gaps in AI capabilities， leading to a more comprehensive understanding of technology’s role and limitations. This holistic approach not only enhances their cognitive abilities but also prepares them for responsible and informed use of AI in their future endeavors. INTRODUCTION 29 Overview of AI Ethics: Understanding the Conversation Artificial intelligence often seems to progress rapidly， as though it is a natural phenomenon that unfolds over time. However， AI is unlike the changing of seasons or biological phenomena in that the driving force behind AI is people – developers， researchers， investors， customers， etc. – who collectively fashion the next technological advancement into existence. This human influence introduces various biases， motivations， and incentives into the developmental process. While these innovations could bring great benefits to the creators and the users of AI tools， they also carry potential consequences， ranging from minor inconveniences to profound inequities or harm. AI ethics examines the impact AI systems have on society and determines how to ensure AI is developed and used responsibly. These issues are not just relevant to those with deep knowledge of AI systems to tackle， but everyone that interacts with these systems. Most people who drive cars， for example， probably do not fully understand the inner mechanics of their vehicles， but that does not preclude them having a moral compass about how cars should be used. The same applies to AI: You don’t need to be an AI expert to have a sense of what’s morally right or wrong. Furthermore， most of the advanced AI models are much less transparent about how they make decisions. This lack of transparency can make it difficult to know if AI systems are generating outputs ethically. Hence， it’s important to think about the ethical implications of AI systems， especially when they are used in decision-making tasks. EDUCATORS 37 Teachers’ Considerations Regarding AI Use in Assignments Clarity: Consider， before assigning any work， clearly stating whether AI is allowed and to what extent. This clarity ensures that all students understand the expectations and can adhere to them， fostering a fair and equitable learning environment. Rationale: Consider providing reasons behind decisions on AI use in assignments. Guidance: Consider guiding students on how to use AI responsibly when allowed. This includes teaching students to critically assess AI-generated content and to use AI as a tool for learning enhancement rather than as a shortcut. Support: Consider providing resources for students to learn about AI and its applications. This support ensures that all students， regardless of their prior exposure to AI， can confidently use these tools in their academic work. Establishing a classroom culture that empowers students to use AI tools ethically and responsibly is the responsibility of every educator. Evaluating Student Work It is highly recommended that educators use caution when leveraging AI tools to evaluate student work. When weighing whether to use AI to evaluate student work， educators are asked to consider the following: • Make sure the student work does not have personally identifiable student information. • Communicate with students that you will be leveraging AI to evaluate their work. Using AI Detection Tools It is highly recommended that educators do not utilize AI detection software in evaluating student work. Research by both Vanderbilt University and Stanford University have shown these tools to be less accurate than advertised， as well as biased against non-native English speakers and writers. The best way to detect if AI was used inappropriately within a learning experience is to know your students’ voice and writing style through samples of work gathered over time. Rather than rely on AI detection software， it is recommended that educators create a classroom culture built on the ethical use of AI within the learning journey. If the inappropriate use of AI is suspected， it is recommended that educators have a conversation with the student(s)， allowing them to explain if they used AI and in what compacity within the assignment. If an AI Matrix has been implemented and clearly communicated within the classroom， it can form the basis for these conversations. Ultimately， the goal of these conversations is for both the educator and student to understand the use of AI. OVERVIEW OF AI ETHICS: UNDERSTANDING THE CONVERSATION 38 Students Artificial intelligence is quickly becoming more capable of doing many incredible things. You， as a student， have an important role in making sure that AI is used for good. Here’s why: You are the ultimate AI tester. Being a student means you are great at exploring new things and using AI in creative ways to learn and grow. It’s like playing a game and figuring out all the best moves. You probably already use many applications or websites every day that make use of AI， such as social media， video streaming and recommendation sites， and virtual assistants. Keep in mind that AI is kind of like a toy robot. In some ways， it can be very sophisticated and can perform some complex tasks， but at the same time it can only do what it is programmed to do. This means AI can be used in the wrong way， sometimes by accident. Plus， the companies that make AI might collect your personal information without you knowing it! In other words， there are pros and cons to using AI， which is why it is so important that you engage with AI ethically. Think like a detective. You want information from the AI， but you also have questions to ask yourself， such as: • Is the AI helping you learn or is it just doing the work for you? • What kind of information is the AI using to learn? • Does the application ask for personal information that you would not normally give to a stranger? • Are the results or responses fair or biased? What sort of information might be missing from the results that you think should be considered? • How could someone misuse this tool， either on purpose or by mistake? By critically thinking about AI， you can help make sure it benefits everyone. If you are ever unsure， ask your teachers， family， or community members. Framework for Students on Discussing Their Workflow When working with AI， it’s important to think about people. First， consider how you’re using AI. Is it helping you with a task? Maybe suggesting what to write in an essay or creating some cool art to show your friends what you are imagining? Keep people and how they will view your work in mind. Next， check the work that AI gives you (output). Whatever writing or picture the software gives you， take a close look and evaluate it. Is it accurate? Does it make sense? If you are unsure， talk to your teacher. When it is time to submit the final project， make sure you have used AI wisely. Contact Information for Ethical Concerns .......................................................................................... 5 Reporting AI Ethical Issues ................................................................................................... 5 Who to Contact for Help ....................................................................................................... 5 Resources for Ethical AI Use .................................................................................................. 6 The SPS Artificial Intelligence (AI) Handbook aims to provide a comprehensive guide for integrating AI into the SPS educational environment. It outlines the benefits of AI in personalizing learning， supporting diverse student needs， and enhancing efficiency. The document emphasizes the importance of community support， equitable access to AI tools， and maintaining a safe and ethical AI environment. It also includes guidelines for responsible AI use， protecting student privacy， and addressing AI misuse. Overall， the handbook seeks to ensure that AI is used effectively and ethically to improve educational outcomes for all students. 1. Introduction What is AI? Artificial Intelligence or AI is a branch of computer science that focuses on creating machines and software that can perform tasks that usually require human intelligence. Artificial Intelligence， or AI， is a part of computer science that works on developing machines and software to perform tasks that typically need human thinking and decision-making. It focuses on creating and using smart tools that can help with things like learning， problem-solving， and making choices. AI impact in Education AI is changing education by making learning more personalized and interactive. For example， AI can help teachers create lessons that fit each student’s needs， making it easier for everyone to understand the material. It can also provide instant feedback on assignments， so students know what they need to improve right away. Additionally， AI tools can help teachers with administrative tasks， giving them more time to focus on teaching. AI holds significant potential to transform the educational experience in the classroom by personalizing learning， providing real-time feedback， and enhancing student engagement through interactive tools and resources. Our Goals with AI in School • Personalized Learning – AI can help create lessons that fit each student’s unique needs. This could mean explaining a math problem several different ways or creating specific problems to help students increase their understanding and close knowledge gaps. • Inclusive Education – AI can support students from different backgrounds by offering tools like language translation and speech recognition. This helps students who speak different languages or have different learning styles to participate fully in class and feel included. • Culturally Responsive Teaching – AI can help teachers create lessons that reflect the diverse cultures of their students. This means using examples， stories， and materials from various cultures to make learning more relatable and respectful of everyone’s background. • Supports Student-Centered High-Quality Instruction- Educators and students should use AI in ways that center student experiences， learning， thinking， and creativity. Additionally， while AI technology can provide significant assistance in educational settings， it is crucial for teachers to refrain from using AI for grading. AI cannot substitute the educator's understanding of their students' abilities and the personalized feedback necessary for fostering student growth. 2. Community Support and Resources Learn about AI Together SPS is focused on fostering community support and providing resources for learning about AI by creating a collaborative environment where students， teachers， parents， and local organizations work together. This can be achieved through workshops with AI experts， access to educational resources， projects applying AI to real- world problems， and engaging parents through informational sessions. These strategies collectively empower everyone to learn about AI together. Find AI Learning Materials Please refer to the public AI website https://www.seattleschools.org/AI or if you’re an employee use the internal web resources. 3. Equal Educational Opportunities Encourage Everyone to Learn AI Decisions to use AI tools will be based on whether they significantly benefit student learning and if any risks can be adequately mitigated. AI tools can be used to aid learning， provide additional resources， and support research. However， they should be used thoughtfully and not as a replacement when a learning opportunity requires critical thinking， original idea creation， deep understanding， or thorough evaluation. Make AI Accessible to All If AI tools are required in courses， they should be available and accessible to all users， to prevent disparities in learning opportunities and future career-connected learning pathways. Accommodations should be made to ensure equitable access to approved AI tools that support teaching and learning. Support Diverse Groups with AI Efforts will be made to assess and address any risks of biased information produced by AI tools. Educators should identify how AI can show bias and lack representation. They must review AI use through an actively anti-racist educator lens and discuss these implications with students to identify paths for students to reflect on and address these issues. 4. Create a Safe AI Environment Keep data private When using AI protect personally identifiable information (PII). Do not share any PII， including name， birth date， address， phone number， social security number， or other financial or confidential information. When asked to provide information think about whether that information is really needed by the requester. Always make sure there's a written agreement in place about how that information can be used. Choose Trustworthy AI Tools We carefully select AI tools that protect our students' privacy. Any outside companies we work with must follow strict data protection rules and comply with FERPA (a law that protects student information). Think Before You Share Before giving any student information to an AI tool， ask yourself， ”Does it really need to know this?” Don't share anything that's not necessary – it's like keeping secrets safe with a good friend. ”Free” AI Tools Might Not Be Free Be careful with AI tools that are free to use. They might collect information about your students， like their messages， files， and feedback. It's like talking to a stranger on the bus – you don't know where your words might end up. Protect Student Privacy When using any AI tool， especially free ones， consider turning off the chat history. This way， your students' conversations won't be saved or used to train the AI. It's like having a private conversation that stays between you and the AI. 5. AI Misuse Guidelines Communication is critical AI tools can enhance learning and foster 21st century skills， but all work using AI tools must center student thinking， creativity， and experiences. Educators should state a clear policy on AI use for their classroom and/or school in syllabus or class rules. They must share this information with students and families， so that they are aware of when and how it is and is not acceptable to use AI in your classroom. AI Misuse Academic Dishonesty/Plagiarism is the deliberate submission of others’ work as one’s own or aiding another in such conduct， along with unauthorized use of sources， as outlined in the SPS’s Student Rights and Responsibilities Handbook. Unauthorized use of AI or ChatGPT without proper citation is considered a breach of this policy， leading to potential disciplinary action. The SPS Discipline Matrix provides for either a classroom-based or school-based response (excluding exclusion) for instances of academic dishonesty/plagiarism. It is recommended that schools revise their discipline policies and student handbooks to explicitly address the unauthorized utilization of AI tools. AI Detectors SPS does not support the use of AI detectors to identify plagiarism or academic dishonesty， since they can produce false positives and false negatives which can damage relationships. Instead， use your professional knowledge of students’ voice， writing development， and classwork to identify academic dishonesty. Educators should consider updating assignments to be more AI-resistant through the suggestions from the University of Chicago and Carleton College. 6. Responsible Use of AI Student Rights with AI Students may use AI on an assignment if the classroom teacher permits. If the teacher has not specifically indicated whether AI is recommended or permitted for an assignment， the student should ask before using AI. Types of AI Permission Levels AI Recommended AI is recommended for use in completing this assignment or project. Students are encouraged to explore AI tools and techniques to enhance their work. Properly cite any AI-generated work products. AI Permitted AI is permitted but not required for completing this assignment or project. Students can choose to use AI tools and techniques if they believe it will improve their work. Properly cite any AI-generated work products. AI Restricted AI use in completing this assignment or project is restricted. Students are expected to complete the work using only their own knowledge and skills. Use AI Responsibly • Use AI ethically: Use AI tools and techniques in a responsible， ethical， and respectful manner. This includes not using AI to cheat， plagiarize， or gain an unfair advantage. Do not use AI to generate offensive， inappropriate， or harmful content. • Understand the limitations of AI: Understand the limitations of AI and recognize that it is not a substitute for critical thinking， creativity， and problem-solving skills. • Consider the potential biases of AI: Be aware that AI tools and techniques may be biased and take steps to mitigate bias when using AI. • Check sources generated by AI: AI is not perfect， has been known to create inaccurate information， and can be used to create misinformation and disinformation. Use SIFT research skills (Stop， Investigate the Source， Find Better Coverage & Trace to the Original Context) to check sources and find independent facts to confirm AI-generated content. • Provide attribution: When using AI tools and techniques， provide proper attribution and credit to the source of the tool or technique. • Seek guidance when in doubt: When you are unsure whether the use of AI is appropriate for a particular assignment or project， staff should seek guidance from your building administration， students should seek guidance from the educator. 7. How We Know AI is Working How We Know AI is Working AI is working when it can perform tasks that typically need human experience. At SPS， AI might help teachers by reviewing writing quickly， suggesting personalized learning activities for students， or creating project synopsis using the latest project management framework. We know AI works well when it can do these tasks accurately and efficiently， making things easier for both teachers， students， and support staff. If students are growing and learning and teachers have more time to help students， it’s a good sign that AI is doing its job effectively. SPS may send out surveys to assess how well AI is assisting our staff and students. Success Stories with AI Please contact techline@seattleschools.org with your success stories! 8. Contact Information for Ethical Concerns Reporting AI Ethical Issues If you have questions or concerns about AI: Speak Up! If you're worried about how AI is being used in our schools， we want to hear from you. Whether it's about privacy， fairness， or anything else， don't be afraid to ask questions or share your concerns. Your voice is important! You can submit questions via the SPS AI webpage (https://www.seattleschools.org/ai/). Who to Contact for Help If you need help with something related to AI， here are some people you can reach out to: • Your teachers or school counselor • The school principal • Cybersecurity@seattleschools.org Resources for Ethical AI Use We want students and staff to use AI in a responsible and thoughtful way. Here are some places you can find more information: https://www.seattleschools.org/ai https://www.seattleschools.org/student-portal/technology-supports-for-families/digital-tools/ai-tools/#faq

Handbook. This handbook is designed to help staff， students， and families learn together. It sets the foundation for how we explore and use AI to support learning， creativity， and daily operations， while keeping people， relationships， and sound judgment at the center of everything we do. The purpose of this handbook is to build shared understanding and grow expertise so AI can be used effectively， responsibly， and confidently across our district. We invite everyone to engage by asking questions， trying things out， and learning along the way. You might see AI used as a “teammate” to help draft lesson ideas， analyze data， improve accessibility， support communication， or streamline routine tasks， freeing time for the work that matters most: teaching， learning， problem-solving， and caring for students. Vision: Human-Centered & Future-Ready Bellevue School District will use AI to strengthen human connection in education， giving educators more time to teach， students more personalized support， and our community better tools to learn， work， and lead. Our focus is future-ready learning， making sure our students graduate with the skills， curiosity， and confidence they need to lead and thrive in a rapidly changing world. Our District Guiding Principles 1. People First: We lead with judgment， care， and responsibility， and AI is used in ways that honor our values， protect our community， and serve our educational mission. 2. Fair， Inclusive， & Thoughtful: We use AI in ways that promote fairness， access， and belonging， and we carefully check AI outputs for bias or misinformation. 3. Responsible & Transparent: We are open about when and how AI is used， and people remain accountable for decisions， outcomes， and ethical use. 4. Private & Secure by Design: We protect student and staff data by following privacy laws， security standards， and district guidelines when using AI tools. 5. Future-Ready & Learning-Focused: We build understanding， skills， and shared norms to prepare students and staff for a changing world， and we regularly reflect and adapt our AI use as technology， research， and community needs evolve. AI tools may support our work， but people remain responsible for decisions， relationships， and outcomes Road Map: Building AI Thoughtfully， Together This handbook reflects our current direction， not a final destination. Our road map centers people， learning， and responsibility， and it recognizes that thoughtful implementation requires ongoing dialogue， reflection， and shared ownership across the district. This handbook will continue to grow as technology and our understanding change. Strategic Alignment Our AI road map is grounded in Bellevue School District’s strategic priorities and long-term vision for students， staff， and our community. AI decisions and practices will be aligned to: Last Updated: September 2026 Page 3 • High-quality teaching and learning， supporting academic excellence and meaningful student engagement • Equitable systems and experiences， ensuring technology strengthens access， belonging， and fairness • Strong professional practice， respecting educator expertise and supporting staff • Sustainable and responsible operations， balancing innovation with fiscal responsibility， privacy， and environmental considerations Last Updated: September 2026 Page 4 AI at Bellevue School District Artificial intelligence is changing how work gets done across Bellevue School District. This section provides guidance for the responsible use of AI in operational work and applies to all staff， especially those in administrative， operational， or support roles. It is designed to help staff understand when and how AI may be used， apply district expectations consistently， and feel confident using it in day-to-day work. Aligned with the district’s Strategic Plan and Annual Plan， this guidance supports BSD’s values of We Belong， We Learn， and We Lead by showing how AI can enhance efficiency， communication， and service delivery while maintaining human oversight， equity， and public trust. Bellevue School District is committed to ensuring staff have the knowledge and tools to use AI thoughtfully， responsibly， and in support of long-term district goals， both in their professional roles and beyond. AI tools may support our work， but people remain responsible for decisions， relationships， and outcomes. How AI Can Support Operations Work AI can support staff by assisting with routine， time-consuming， and organizational tasks， helping streamline work while reinforcing the importance of human judgment and accountability. Daily Tasks & Efficiency Use AI to streamline routine work—drafting emails， organizing notes， and summarizing information—so you can spend more time on what matters most. Decision Support—not Decision-Making AI can help surface data， patterns， and options， but final decisions should always rest with a human. Treat AI output as one input among many， not the answer itself. Collaboration & Coordination AI tools can help teams communicate， brainstorm， and stay aligned—but they work best alongside real conversation and relationship-building， not in place of it. Clarity， Accessibility， & Equity Use AI to make information clearer and more accessible for all audiences， while staying mindful of bias， accuracy， and equitable access to these tools. Human Responsibility and Public Records AI is a support tool， not a substitute for people. Work created with AI as part of district business may be considered a public record. Staff should consult district public records and retention guidance and use AI thoughtfully and responsibly. Transparency & Communication Transparency is essential to build trust with students， families， staff， and the broader community. When AI tools are used in district work， staff should communicate clearly and responsibly—especially when AI contributes to communications， materials， or decision support. AI may assist the work， but people remain responsible for accuracy， tone， decisions， and outcomes. Be transparent when it matters • If staff use AI to generate， revise， summarize， or translate content in a way that goes beyond minor edits， they should be prepared to explain how it was used. • Transparency and disclosure are especially important when: AI plays a significant role in family-facing or public communications o Last Updated: September 2026 Page 5 Materials are widely shared， published， or used for guidance o Content informs reports， summaries， or recommendations shared with leadership o Stakeholders would reasonably expect to know how the content was created o Maintain human voice and responsibility • All AI-assisted content must be reviewed， edited， and approved by staff before sharing. • Communications should reflect district tone， context， and values， not automated language. • Staff remain accountable for all content distributed. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 6 Privacy How the District Uses AI Safely and Responsibly The district may use artificial intelligence tools to support learning， communication， and day-to-day operations. When we do， protecting student and staff information is a top priority. Below is a clear explanation of how we safeguard data and respect privacy. Protecting Student and Staff Information When AI tools are used， the district takes steps to protect students， staff， and district information from misuse， leaks， or unauthorized access. Any use of AI must follow existing district technology and privacy rules， as well as federal and state privacy laws， including laws that protect student education records. Using Only the Information That Is Necessary We limit the amount of information shared with AI tools. • Staff are encouraged to use summaries or examples instead of full student records. • Whenever possible， information is removed， changed， or made anonymous before it is used. • AI tools should be given only what is needed to complete a task， nothing more. Keeping AI Tools Secure AI tools are not connected to school systems like email， grading systems， or payroll unless the district’s IT department has approved it. This helps reduce the risk of data breaches or account compromise. All AI use must meet the district’s cybersecurity and technology use standards. Protecting Personal Information Personal information must always be handled carefully when using AI tools. Personal information includes things like: • Student names， ID numbers， or photos • Grades， attendance， or discipline records • Health or special education information • Staff personnel records This type of information is not entered into public or consumer AI tools unless the district has approved it. Even small pieces of information can sometimes identify a person when combined with other details， so care is taken to avoid that. NOTE: Microsoft Copilot Chat is the only district-approved AI tool for use with personal， confidential， or private information， and staff must not enter this type of information into any other AI tool. Following Privacy Laws (FERPA) All uses of AI follow the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and other privacy laws. • Student education records are only shared when legally allowed—such as with family permission or for a valid educational reason. • If a vendor’s AI system uses student data， the vendor must follow strict rules and can only use that data for approved educational purposes under district control. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 7 Being Transparent with Families We believe trust comes from openness. • The district will clearly explain when AI tools are used， why they are used， and how information is protected. • Staff are expected to be able to explain AI use in classrooms or district operations in plain， understandable terms. Resources: • 2022P: Electronic Resources - Student Acceptable Use of District Network • 6800.2P: Acceptable Use • FAMILY EDUCATIONAL RIGHTS AND PRIVACY Last Updated: September 2026 Page 8 Governance and Oversight This section explains how decisions about AI tools are made， who is responsible， and how the district ensures AI is used responsibly. Governance helps protect students， staff， and the district by setting clear rules and processes for AI use. Roles and Responsibilities Using AI responsibly is a shared responsibility across the district. Role Responsibilities Staff • Use only district-approved AI tools • Follow district expectations for privacy， safety， and data protection • Report concerns， risks， or misuse when identified School & Department • Support responsible AI use in their buildings or teams Leaders • Ensure staff follow district guidance and expectations • Elevate concerns， questions， or requests when needed AI Leadership Team • Provide strategic oversight to support intentional， ethical AI use aligned with district goals • Review risks， proposed tools and use cases， compliance needs， and updates to guidance and policy Data Governance and Systems Data governance includes key areas such as acceptable use， student records and privacy， information security， records management， and incident response. These areas are covered by other resources: • 2022P: Electronic Resources - Student Acceptable Use of District Network • 6800.2P: Acceptable Use • 3231P: Student Records • FAMILY EDUCATIONAL RIGHTS AND PRIVACY Overview of AI Tools in Use Bellevue School District uses a set of approved AI tools that have been reviewed for privacy， security， educational or operational value， and alignment with district values， and that include safeguards for student and staff data. Approved tools include Magic School， Colleague AI and Microsoft Copilot. Microsoft Copilot Chat is the only district-approved AI tool for use with personal， confidential， or private information， and staff must not enter this type of information into any other AI tool. Staff should not use personal or unapproved AI tools for school or district business unless explicitly authorized. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 9 Procurement and Vendor Requirements All AI tools must follow district procurement and vendor review processes. Before approval， vendors must meet district privacy， security， and legal requirements， including signing data privacy agreements and clearly explaining how district data is collected， stored， deleted， and protected. Vendors may not use district data to train AI models unless explicitly authorized by the district. AI tools may not be purchased or adopted outside of established district processes (6210P: Purchasing Authorization and Control). AI Tool Evaluation and Approval Process Bellevue School District uses a formal process to review and approve AI tools. The approval process includes: 1. A request is submitted for a new AI tool. 2. The tool is reviewed for data protection， legal compliance， security， educational or operational value， and equity and accessibility considerations. 3. A decision is made and communicated Approval is required before an AI tool is used with students or district data. Monitoring and Re-evaluating AI Tools Approved AI tools are monitored over time for vendor or policy changes， reported concerns， and continued alignment with district expectations. If concerns arise or a tool is no longer appropriate for district use， it may be restricted， re-evaluated， paused， or removed， and the district will communicate expectations to staff， address data retention or deletion， and update the approved tools list. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 10 Teaching & Learning with Generative AI The Big 3: What They Mean & Why They Matter Generative AI Big 3 1. Be Transparent Disclose how you used AI. Share your process， not just your product. 2. Think Critically Verify， question， and evaluate AI outputs before accepting or sharing. 3. Create Responsibly Use AI to expand your thinking and deepen your learning， not to replace it. Why these matter: • Connect to digital citizenship and ethical technology use • Support college， career， and life readiness • Reflect BSD values: integrity， curiosity， and responsible innovation Shared language: • Used consistently in classrooms， assignments， and feedback • Reinforced in conversations with students and families • The Big 3 are durable principles， not tied to any specific tool. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 11 Risks and Responsibilities in Teaching & Learning Transparency means naming risks honestly. These are not reasons to avoid AI. They are reasons to approach it with the Big 3. Risk Summary Over-reliance When AI does the thinking， students lose the practice， undermining independent problem-solving and content mastery. Misinformation & AI generates confident-sounding falsehoods. AI output must always Hallucinations be verified before use. Algorithmic Bias & AI trained on historical data can reflect existing biases， Inequity disadvantaging students of color， MLLs， students with disabilities， and low-income communities. Data Privacy Personally identifiable student information must never be entered into tools that have not been reviewed and approved by BSD. Academic Dishonesty AI makes it easy to submit work that doesn't reflect a student's own understanding， undermining the value of learning. Equity & Access Gaps Unequal access to devices and tools can widen achievement gaps if implementation is not thoughtful and equitable. Developmental The appropriate role of AI differs by age. Passive AI use and Considerations screen time carry developmental risks， particularly in K–5. Emotional & Social Over-reliance on AI for feedback or affirmation can hinder resilience Development and authentic relationship development. Human Oversight AI supports decision-making; it never replaces educator professional judgment. AI must not be the sole input for high-stakes decisions. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 12 Possibilities of AI in Teaching & Learning When aligned with the Big 3， AI expands access， efficiency， and creativity. Possibility What It Looks Like Differentiation & Meeting learners where they are: adapting pace， depth， and modality to P ersonalization individual needs. Culturally Surfacing diverse perspectives， materials， and representation across Responsive curriculum. T eaching High-Quality Supporting lesson design， resource creation， and intellectual rigor. I nstruction E fficiency Reducing administrative burden so educators can focus on relationships and learning. T imely Feedback Faster feedback loops for students; formative insights for teachers. Personalized AI as a patient， on-demand thought partner for students. C oaching Emerging This space will expand as the field evolves and BSD continues to learn. P ossibilities Last Updated: September 2026 Page 13 Student Use of AI The Big 3 in student practice: concrete expectations， clear examples， and honest conversations. Common Language & The Big 3 in Action Students use the Big 3 as a shared vocabulary across all classrooms and grade levels. Transparency， critical thinking， and responsible creation describe expected practice in real student work. Classroom Generative AI Guidelines To help students know when and how AI tools fit into their classwork， our classrooms display a simple stoplight guide. Just like a real stoplight， it gives students a quick， visual signal for how much AI support is appropriate for a given assignment. Red — No AI Assistance Complete all work independently Yellow — Okay to Use AI as an Assistant AI can help organize ideas， give feedback， and coach when stuck (must cite use) Green — Human-AI Partnership Research or create in collaboration with AI (must explain process) Teachers will let students know which ”light” applies to each assignment， so students always have clear expectations for how AI can (or can't) be part of their work. Authorship & Academic Integrity Students remain the author when AI is involved. Voice， ownership， and originality still matter. Existing academic integrity policies apply to AI use; students use the Generative AI Disclosure form to document their process. Students should clearly indicate: • Whether AI was used • Which tools were used • How AI contributed (brainstorming， feedback， etc.) • That they are responsible for final content Generative AI Disclosure Gemini o o I did not use AI tools for this o Other: __________ assignment. I used AI for: I used the following AI tool(s): Brainstorming / Idea Generation o o Magic School o Feedback， Editing， or Revision o ColleagueAI o Organization or Outlining o Copilot o Multimedia Generation o Canva o Other (briefly describe): __________ o Claude Initial: ____ — I reviewed all AI-supported work ChatGPT and am responsible for the final content o submitted. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 14 Helpful vs. Unhelpful Uses Helpful: supports learning Unhelpful: undermines learning Using AI to brainstorm， then doing the writing Submitting AI-generated text as your own work yourself Asking AI to explain a concept you're stuck on Asking AI to complete an assignment for you Using AI feedback to revise your draft Replacing your own thinking with AI's thinking Checking AI output against reliable sources Accepting AI output as fact without verification AI， Productive Struggle & Persistence Working through challenges is how learning happens. Students are encouraged to use AI to get unstuck， not to skip the struggle. The discomfort of not knowing yet is part of growth. Students should understand: • AI can be inaccurate， biased， or incomplete • Not all uses of AI are appropriate in all assignments • Their learning， not just the final product， is the goal • Responsible use protects their credibility and growth Educator Use of AI Educators are held to the same Big 3 expectations they teach. The framework mirrors the student section intentionally. Helpful Educator Uses Unhelpful Educator Uses Using AI to generate lesson plan drafts for review Publishing AI-generated materials without review or disclosure Using AI to create differentiated versions of Using AI to write individualized student resources communications without oversight Using AI for feedback on your own writing Relying on AI for high-stakes student decisions Disclosing AI use in materials shared with Entering student PII (personally identifiable families information) into non-approved AI tools Educators disclose AI use in professional materials and apply the same critical evaluation expected of students. Professional judgment remains the non-negotiable safeguard. Educators are responsible for: • Accuracy and quality of all materials • Alignment to instructional goals Last Updated: September 2026 Page 15 • Maintaining student privacy • Modeling ethical and transparent AI use Assessment， Feedback & Academic Integrity Transparency is the standard. When students and educators practice the Big 3， most integrity questions are resolved before they become conflicts. Using AI Productively in Assessment & Feedback AI can play a supportive role in the following formative contexts: Context How AI Can Help Formative feedback Generate initial feedback drafts for educator review before sharing with students. Rubric support Draft rubrics aligned to learning targets; educators review and finalize. Student self-assessment AI can prompt reflection questions or provide coaching as students assess their own work. Data pattern review Summarizing aggregate (non-PII) assessment data to support instructional planning. Where AI Must Not Be Used in Assessment The following high-stakes determinations require human judgment. AI must not be the sole or primary input: Category Examples Final grades Summative grades， course credit， GPA-impacting marks Individualized plans IEP， 504， ELL， behavior support decisions Discipline Suspensions， expulsions， behavioral consequences Placement & advancement Grade retention， course placement， intervention assignment Responding to Suspected Misuse BSD takes a process-centered approach to suspected AI misuse. Educators should: • Start with a conversation. Ask the student to explain their process， thinking， and choices. • Consult the AI Disclosure form if one was submitted. • Apply existing academic integrity policy; AI misuse is not categorically different from other forms of dishonesty. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 16 • Document the concern and follow building-level procedures. • Avoid relying on AI detection tools as primary evidence. Student & Family Response Students have the right to a fair process. If a student believes they have been incorrectly accused of AI misuse， they should: • Share any evidence of their process (drafts， notes， conversation history， disclosure forms). • Request a conversation with the educator and， if needed， a school counselor or administrator. Families can support by talking with their student about how they used AI， reviewing submitted disclosure forms， and contacting the school with questions or concerns. Teaching Authorship， Originality & AI Use These conversations belong in instruction， not just policy. Recommended practices: • Explicitly teach what authorship means when AI is a collaborator. • Design assignments that make process visible， such as drafts， reflections， or annotations. • Use the AI Disclosure form as a teaching tool， not just an accountability measure. • Model your own transparency as an educator when you use AI to prepare materials. Citation & Transparency Practices The Generative AI Disclosure form (see section 4， above) is the district's standard tool for documenting AI use in student and educator work. It captures: • Whether AI was used at all. • Which tool(s) were used. • What the AI was used for (brainstorming， feedback， drafting， etc.). • A student acknowledgment of responsibility for the final product. Educators may additionally ask students to submit prompts used， AI conversation logs， or written reflections on how AI shaped their process. Process evidence (drafts， reflections， conversation history， and the student's ability to discuss their work) is more reliable and more equitable. Last Updated: September 2026 Page 17

title: Artificial Intelligence (Tacoma Public Schools)
full_text: Artificial Intelligence Tacoma Public Schools empowers students and educators to use AI tools in ways that enhance learning， inspire creativity， and prepare students for college， careers， and civic engagement. The use of AI in the classroom prepares students to become responsible digital citizens in a fast-changing world. Copilot and Colleague AI available to most secondary students TPS students have access to two AI tools. Microsoft Copilot is available to students in grades 8-12. This tool is a chatbot available in the Edge internet browser on student laptops and helps students with research， writing， and problem-solving while maintaining academic integrity standards. Colleague AI is available to students in grades 6-12 and is a tool set up by the classroom teacher to provide learning and tutoring support. AI tools in the classroom Artificial Intelligence is used across many platforms in the district to support learning， creativity， and productivity. The following is a summary of applications and/or tools that are available to students: Microsoft Copilot : Chatbot available in the Edge browser. Colleague AI : Tool that provides learning and tutoring support for students. Canva : Tools such as Magic Write， Magic Studio， Magic Design， and Magic Media Nearpod， Flip， Kami， and Clipchamp : AI features for creating questions， assignments， videos， and more. Search engines like Google also use AI to deliver smarter search results， autocomplete suggestions， and personalized recommendations. AI is now integrated into daily tools - not just chatbots - assisting students and staff to work more efficiently and creatively. What is Microsoft Copilot? What is Colleague AI? How has the district prepared for using AI? Why is the district using AI? How can students use AI to help with assignments? What are some examples of appropriate use? How can families help students use AI appropriately? What district policies and regulations support AI use? Copilot is a Microsoft-powered AI chatbot. This tool is available to students in grades 8-12. The chatbot assists with writing， brainstorming， summarizing， and other academic tasks. The following safeguards are built into the chatbot by Microsoft: Age-based filtering for inappropriate content Privacy protections aligned with Microsoft’s education standards No data sharing with advertisers or third parties Copilot is available on student laptops through the Edge internet browser. Colleague AI is designed for classroom use only. This tool is available to students in grades 6-12 and provides tutoring-style support by guiding students through ideas， offering feedback， and helping students think critically. The tool actively monitors for safety by filtering for prompts like self-harm， abuse， and threats. Notifications are sent to teachers and school counselors when inappropriate content is detected and flagged. Colleague AI is only available to students in the classroom. Students cannot access independently unless set up by a teacher. The district has spent over two years preparing to implement AI in ways that are safe， responsible， and supportive of student learning. This work has involved teachers， students， families， and community partners. The following are examples of the work and collaboration leading up to using AI in the classroom: Listening Sessions : Families， staff， and community members were invited to share their hopes， concerns， and questions about AI. Their feedback helped shape the district’s implementation plan and communication. AI Committee : A team of educators and leaders created a clear vision and plan for integrating AI in classrooms， emphasizing ethics， inclusion， and student success. Teacher Training : Staff received professional development on how to use AI tools responsibly and effectively to support learning and teaching. Prepared Students : Before the Oct. 20 launch of Copilot and Colleague AI tools， students complete a required lesson that teaches responsible use， safety， and digital citizenship. Policies， Regulations， and District Handbook : The district revised its student handbook and technology policies to clearly outline expectations for safe and appropriate AI use. Strategic Partnerships : Tacoma collaborated with organizations such as Microsoft， Colleague AI， and the University of Washington to co-create tools and increase access. These collaborations helped lower costs and enhanced usability for staff and students. These efforts ensure AI is used to enhance learning while protecting student safety， privacy， and academic integrity. Tacoma Public Schools collaborates with teachers， students， and families to ensure AI is used safely and responsibly. The goal is to empower students and educators to: help students become responsible digital citizens who are prepared for college， careers， and civic life， this reflects the district’s long-term mission to prepare students for success beyond school. promote the ethical use of AI ， ensure all students have access to safe， fair， and meaningful learning experiences with AI. make learning more engaging and personalized for students， supports day-to-day classroom instruction and meets diverse learning needs. promote creativity and innovation in the classroom， it encourages exploration， imagination， and future-ready thinking. Students should follow their teacher’s guidelines and use AI as a tool to support learning， not a shortcut. Here's a helpful guide from our teacher training that outlines different levels of AI use approved by the teacher: 0% AI Use : No AI allowed (e.g.， personal reflections， assessments) 25% AI Use : AI for brainstorming or generating ideas 50% AI Use : AI used for drafting， with student revision and reflection 75% AI Use : AI used for structure and support， with student input and editing 100% AI Use : Content generated by AI with student review， reflection， and teacher approval Using AI responsibly involves using it as a tool to enhance learning and understanding. Appropriate Use: Asking AI to help brainstorm ideas for a science project. Using AI to summarize a long article before writing a response. Getting feedback on grammar or sentence structure. Translating complex language for better understanding. Inappropriate Use: Asking AI to write an entire essay and submitting it as your own. Using AI to cheat on tests or assignments. Asking AI about harmful or unsafe topics. By using AI responsibly， students can benefit from its capabilities while maintaining academic integrity and safety. Parents can play an important role in guiding their children to use AI responsibly. Here are some ways families can encourage proper AI use: Engage in Conversations : Talk with your child about how they’re using AI in school and what they’ve learned from classroom lessons on responsible use. Reinforce AI as a Learning Tool : Stress that AI is meant to assist learning， not serve as a shortcut or substitute for individual effort. Explore Together : Spend time exploring AI tools together at home and discuss what feels helpful or concerning. By staying involved and informed， parents can help ensure their children use AI in ways that support their learning and development. Use Reliable Resources : Ensure you rely on trusted sources for information and guidance on AI use. Teaching How AI Works to K-8 Students Edutopia: Teaching Students to Use AI Responsibly ISTE: 5 Tips for Using AI in the Classroom Edutopia: Defining Acceptable AI Use Edutopia: AI Literacy for Students Tacoma Public Schools has revised its District Handbook， policies， and regulations to ensure responsible and ethical AI use in classrooms. These updates include: District Handbook : Outlined in the District Handbook， including guided AI lesson for all secondary students involved， and confirming that they understand the district handbook and AI guidance. Policy 2022 and 2022R : Covers acceptable and unacceptable use of digital tools， including AI， with an emphasis on educational purpose， safety， and integrity. 2022 - Electronic Resources and Internet Safety and 2022R - Electronic Resources and Internet Safety Policy 6300 and 6300R : Emphasizes data security and responsible technology use， including AI. 6300 - Data Security and 6300R - Data Security OSPI Resources The Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) provides students， educators， and school district administrators with the resources and tools they need to understand how to use these technologies effectively， ethically， and safely. title: AI Vision (Highline Public Schools)
full_text: AI VISION Highline Public Schools AI Ambassadors – June 2025 Building a Future-Ready Educational Community Highline Public Schools is creating a future-ready educational environment by thoughtfully integrating generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into teaching and learning. Highline’s Promise — every student in Highline Public Schools is known by name， strength and need， and graduates prepared for the future they choose — guides our intentional integration of AI. We view AI as a valuable tool to foster human connections， deepen empathy， promote critical thinking， and enrich educational interactions among students， educators， and families. UDL: The Foundation Central to our educational philosophy is Universal Design for Learning (UDL)， a framework that informs our strategic use of AI. Guided by UDL principles， our implementation of AI ensures multiple means of representation， allowing students to access information in ways that best align with their individual strengths and learning preferences. Additionally， AI facilitates diverse means of action and expression， empowering students to demonstrate their knowledge through various methods suited to their abilities. Furthermore， AI technologies support multiple means of engagement， promoting active and meaningful participation， and sustaining student interest through personalized and inclusive learning experiences. Equity， Safety and Human Connection We believe AI should complement and enhance human interactions rather than replace them. By automating routine tasks and generating insightful data， AI enables educators to concentrate on more meaningful， personalized instruction， thereby strengthening relationships and supporting deeper educational outcomes. Safety and security remain critical aspects of our AI strategy. We prioritize robust data privacy and cybersecurity measures to protect student information and ensure safe digital environments. Ethical considerations and transparency guide our use of AI， supported by rigorous human oversight， ongoing evaluation and regular community discussions. This framework allows us to proactively address privacy concerns， identify and correct algorithmic bias—particularly biases that may disproportionately affect historically underrepresented groups—and uphold principles of fairness. Equity and inclusion are foundational to our AI initiatives. Through careful deployment and continuous monitoring of AI technologies， we aim to dismantle educational barriers and offer equitable learning opportunities for all students， particularly those from historically underserved backgrounds. We remain committed to the ongoing evaluation of AI systems to detect and mitigate algorithmic biases， ensuring that our educational resources foster genuine inclusivity. Preparing Students for a Changing World Our AI vision is aligned with our district’s core educational goals. AI supports a culture of belonging by helping educators better understand and respond to individual student needs， fostering supportive and inclusive environments. It promotes innovative learning through differentiated instruction， real-time feedback， and creative student engagement. AI also significantly enhances bilingual and biliterate competencies， offering advanced language learning tools， translation capabilities， and fostering greater cultural responsiveness. Furthermore， AI prepares students to thrive in the future by cultivating critical digital literacy， ethical technology usage， and adaptive skills essential in a rapidly evolving global society. We invite every member of the Highline community to be part of this shared journey. Together， through thoughtful， ethical， and inclusive applications of AI， we aim to preserve and enhance the profoundly human nature of education， preparing every community member for a successful and dynamic future.
